title: The contagion of fear
author: The Observation Deck
summary:
I have a difficult confession to make — a shameful incident that I have never spoken of, even to those closest to me.
Late one night in my first year at university and having found computer science to be my life’s calling, I was in the back of the large computer science lab, talking with some fellow underclassmen. We were snidely decrying the lack of technological understanding in the broader population, with the kind of arrogance and hubris that youth and precociousness can uniquely summon. Somewhere in this discussion, a terrible idea was hatched: what if we went next door to the general computer lab, and told the humanities students there that a computer virus was spreading through their machines? Would they believe it?

title: I spent 48 hours in SF hanging out with billionaires...
author: GREG ISENBERG
summary:
I spent 48 hours in SF hanging out with billionaires, data labs and AI founders and execs running $1B to $100B companies.

My observations:

1. Sooo MANY stories of data brokers making like $2M a WEEK selling company data to labs. I can't tell if it's the beginning or a bubble, and I kept wondering which niches are left. Digging into it actively.

2. At dinner, someone asked the table, "If a new model drops next month, does your company get better or worse?" HALF the table went quiet! I think that's the best question to ask about any AI startup right now.

3. The bar people talk about now is hitting $1B in revenue in 12 months (I guess that's the new unicorn?). What I didn't hear much about is retention. AI revenue can come in fast and leave fast, and I think we're going to see a lot of stories of AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.

4. It's pretty clear we're living through the reinvention of the computer. The model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system, and skills and plugins are the apps. Thinking about it that way makes it easier to see where the whitespace is.

5. We're maybe 12 months from an agent that can watch you work for a week and then do your job without any instructions. The screen recording plus agent memory plus local model combination makes this possible right now.

6. Agent harnesses feel like the new GPT wrappers, in a good way, especially vertical ones. The best teams I talked to treat the model as swappable. One founder walked me through routing different models to different jobs: one for taste and visuals, a cheaper one for the everyday stuff, another for text. 

They use prompts they can move across models over fine-tuning, and A/B test the output on what users actually do with it: do they edit it, export it, share it? What is AI? What is AI for, and what are its goals? Can we use AI for programming? The dominant discourse in 2025 makes it easy to believe in 2025 that AI is unequivocally good, and will make our lives much easier.

title: I'm done coding with AI
author: Brett Codes
summary:
I decided to stop using AI for coding at my job, even if it costs me that job. I don't know what the future will bring, but I know it will be one where I don't use AI for anything, especially coding at my day job.

Read my less ramble-y thoughts: https://brettcodes.com/im-done-using-ai/

I've been coding for 20 years, and the last 18 months have made me question the career and craft I enjoy so much. Using AI for coding led me to apathy, existential dread, and depression. It made me a worse developer, and it leads to worse software. The way that we as an industry and the entirety of humanity are largely approaching this technology is extremely concerning, and I want to share my experiences and thoughts on it.

Remember your first HTTPS server? RSA keys, year+ certificates, and some openssl incantation you copied from StackOverflow. That's all outdated now.

TLS 1.3 threw out decades of cipher complexity. Snowden leaks moved Perfect Forward Secrecy from optional to mandatory. Let's Encrypt made certificates a free API call. And browser vendors are pushing certificate lifetimes down to 47 days.

This talk is a tour of modern ~~SSL~~ TLS. We'll cover what changed, why it changed, and what breaks if you don't make updates.

author: Devoxx
summary:

Subscribe to LinkedIn @ https://www.linkedin.com/company/voxxed-days-amsterdam

JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) are everywhere—frontends, backends, microservices—and for good reason: they're easy to pass around, self-contained, and standardized. But while JWTs can be a solid fit for authentication, using them for authorization is a decision that comes with serious pitfalls—especially in distributed systems.

In this lightning talk, we’ll explore the technical and security limitations of JWT-based authorization and explain why they're fundamentally incompatible with the needs of modern applications. From the infamous "New Enemy Problem" described in Google’s Zanzibar paper to the vague semantics of scope claims and the difficulty of revoking tokens in-flight, we’ll unpack the real-world consequences of treating JWTs as your AuthZ layer.

title: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
author: Lilian Weng
summary:
The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965), where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence.
This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system, which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs (Anthropic; OpenAI).

title: GitOps Best Practices I Wish I Had Known Before
author: Engin Diri
summary:
Getting started with GitOps can feel like trying to herd cats through a YAML factory while the factory is on fire. It’s one of those things that seems like it ought to be simple (just use Git!), but in practice is much more complex — and you may not realize how much more complex until you’re weeks or more into a project. After years of running GitOps workflows in production across dozens of clusters, I’ve collected a list of best practices that I’m hoping can save you from having to make many of the mistakes I’ve made. Think of it as the GitOps cheat sheet I wish I’d had from Day 1.
If you’re not familiar with the formal definition, the OpenGitOps project distills it into four principles:

Declarative desired state
Versioned and immutable storage
Automatic pulling
Continuous reconciliation

But those principles only define the what. This post is also about the how — the practical lessons that can make or break a GitOps implementation.
In this post, I’ll walk you through the GitOps best practices I’ve picked up from production experience, community talks, and more than a few late-night incident calls. Whether you’re just getting started with GitOps or looking to level up, these tips should help you avoid the potholes.

Git is your single source of truth (no, really)
Declarative over imperative, always
Pull-based deployments are the way
Separate app code from deployment config (when it hurts not to)
Use directories, not branches, for environments
Validate before you merge
Tag with commit SHAs, not “latest”
Automate drift detection and reconciliation
Practice progressive delivery
Policy-as-code: your automated guardrails
Bridge your IaC and GitOps (don’t choose one)
Be pragmatic, not dogmatic


The GitOps mindset in a nutshell.


1. Git is your single source of truth (no, really)
This is the bedrock that the principles of GitOps are built on: every piece of your environment’s desired state lives in a Git repository. No exceptions. No “I’ll just fix it real quick wi...

title: Software That Debugs Itself While I Sleep
author: Tomasz Tunguz
summary:
This week I chatted with an acquaintance who mentioned a board game. I caught half the title & looked for the full title & Amazon link using my AI in Asana.






The system tried with Gemini & failed. The failover to Claude also failed. Rather than continuously iterating with the AI until it worked, I created a Ralph Wiggum loop.
Geoffrey Huntley coined this pattern. Named after the persistently clueless Simpsons character, the idea is simple : keep pushing the model against its failures until it dreams a correct solution just to escape the loop. The system is deterministically bad in an undeterministic world. Iteration beats perfection.



Now an AI loop runs each night. It finds all tasks with “failed” in them. It creates a plan to debug & iterates until the prompt solves the task.
So far this naive system is working pretty well. There is a risk it might begin to oscillate between two optimal states, but I haven’t observed that in the few days it’s been running. It’s something I’m watching.
AI creates software cheaply; excellence requires iteration. Implicit feedback loops are how you get there.
This self improving loop ensures the system wakes up smarter than it went to sleep. So do I.

These are my opinions and are ruminations on what might be happening as more and more developers use LLMs and Frameworks to build on the web.
In October last year I wrote “will developers care about frameworks in the future?” predicting that LLMs would abstract away framework choice. I was wrong—or at least, wrong about the timeline.
The reality is more interesting and more permanent: React isn’t competing with other frameworks anymore. React has become the platform. And if you’re building a new framework, library or browser feature today, you need to understand that you’re not just competing with React—you’re competing against a self-reinforcing feedback loop between LLM training data, system prompts, and developer output that makes displacing React functionally impossible.

title: Open APIs Are Over
author: Tomasz Tunguz
summary:
Salesforce, Datadog & Epic are building walls. After two decades of flourishing through open APIs & data portability, the software industry’s largest incumbents are locking down.
Salesforce restricted Slack’s API1 in May 2025, limiting third-party apps to one API call per minute & fifteen messages per request. Datadog deactivated accounts2 for Deductive AI, a competing observability startup. Epic faces a Texas lawsuit3 accusing it of turning patient records into a “gatekeeping tool.”
The pace of software development, as a result of AI, is accelerating, enabling incumbents to broaden their suite & compete with previous partners. Faster execution means more defense from those with established businesses. This is the new normal.
Platform businesses have minted billions in the past. Vlocity ($1.33B acquisition)4 & Veeva ($36B market cap)5 built multi-billion dollar businesses on the Salesforce platform. nCino reached a $2.9B market cap6 serving financial services on Salesforce. ServiceMax sold to GE Digital for $915M7. Klaviyo built a $8.8B business8 with 78% of its revenue from Shopify customers.
But building on top of a system of record offers less stable ground than it once did. When Salesforce throttles Slack’s API, they’re telegraphing where the value is. When Epic locks down patient records, they’re drawing a map. Incumbents don’t build walls around worthless assets. And they don’t build defenses unless they perceive credible & urgent challengers.
AI’s speed enables both startups & incumbents to own a stack end-to-end. That’s offense in an era of walls.

title: Eleven Steps to the Epiphany[^1]
author: Tomasz Tunguz
summary:
I asked Claude Cowork to read my tools folder. Eleven steps later, it understood how I work.



Over the past year, I built a personal operating system inside Claude Code : scripts to send email, update our CRM, research startups, draft replies. Dozens of small tools wired together. All of it lived in a folder on my laptop, accessible only through the terminal.
Cowork read that folder, parsed each script, & added them to its memory. Now I can do everything I did yesterday, but in a different interface. The capabilities transferred. The container didn’t matter.
My tools don’t belong to the application anymore. They’re portable. In the enterprise, this means laptops given to new employees would have Cowork installed plus a collection of tools specific to each role : the accounting suite, the customer support suite, the executive suite.
The name choice must have been deliberate. Microsoft trained us on copilot for three years : an assistant in the passenger seat, helpful but subordinate. Anthropic chose cowork. You’re working with someone who remembers how you like things done.
We’re entering an era where you just tell the computer what to do. Here’s all my stuff. Here are the five things we need to do today. When we need to see something, a chart, a document, a prototype, an interface will appear on demand.
The current version of Cowork is rough. It’s slow. It crashed twice on startup. It changed the authorization settings for my Claude Code installation. But the promised power is enough to plow through.

title: De-slopify your README files and other documentation with this handy...
author: Jeffrey Emanuel
summary:
De-slopify your README files and other documentation with this handy prompt for Claude Code and Codex:

---

I want you to read through the complete text carefully and look for any telltale signs of "AI slop" style writing; one big tell is the use of emdash. You should try to replace this with a semicolon, a comma, or just recast the sentence accordingly so it sounds good while avoiding emdash. 

Also, you want to avoid certain telltale writing tropes, like sentences of the form "It's not [just] XYZ, it's ABC" or "Here's why" or "Here's why it matters:".  Basically, anything that sounds like the kind of thing an LLM would write disproportionately more commonly that a human writer and which sounds inauthentic/cringe.

And you can't do this sort of thing using regex or a script, you MUST manually read each line of the text and revise it manually in a systematic, methodical, diligent way. Use ultrathink.

title: Celebrating Git's 20th anniversary with creator Linus Torvalds
author: Patrick Steinhardt
summary: The Git version control system was first released on April 7, 2005, by the father of the Linux kernel, Linus Torvalds. To mark the 20th anniversary of this important project that is nowadays used by almost every single developer, I interviewed Linus about the history of Git, why he handed over maintainership of Git, and what he considers to be its most important milestones. In 2005, you were already the maintainer of the thriving Linux kernel. Why did you decide to start a new version control system? So, I got into it from really despising version control. I had used the traditional version control systems (CVS/RCS/SCCS) both as an end user (i.e., tracking open source projects like GCC) and as a developer (we used CVS at Transmeta for everything) and absolutely hated the experience with a passion. And yes, back then most projects that used CVS had probably moved to SVN, but honestly, I always felt that SVN was just "lipstick on a pig." It was just CVS in another form, with some UI improvements, but none of the fundamentals fixed, and a few new problems added. The problems with CVS and its ilk are too many to even list, and, happily, they have largely become irrelevant and younger developers have probably never even had to deal with any of it. I absolutely refused to deal with it for the kernel, even though a few subsystems (notably the networking side) were actually using CVS to track their code back in the '90s. Anyway, back then I lived in the Bay Area, and Larry McVoy, who I knew from other projects (mainly lmbench), had started BitMover, which had a new version control model called BitKeeper, or BK, for short. BK wasn't open source, but Larry liked open source projects and really felt that the lack of version control was holding the kernel back. author: Andreas Papadopulos
summary:
Zelenskyj byl v týdnu ve Varšavě a jeho návštěva zanechala kromě jiného i jakousi nepříjemnou pachuť. 

Polsko čekají v květnu prezidentské volby. Hlavní favoriti jsou dva - vládní Občanská koalice má primátora Varšavy Trzaskowského, opoziční Právo a Spravedlnost má historika Nawrockého. 

Zatímco Trzaskowskému Zelenskyj během návštěvy předal ocenění (ocenění pro celou Varšavu za to, jak přijala válečné uprchlíky), o Nawrockém se ukrajinská hlava státu poměrně arogantně vyjádřila v rozhovoru pro polská média ("Jak že se jmenuje ten pán?" "Nawrocki" "Aha, pardon, tak Nawrocki") a připomněla mu, že pokud Polsko nebude podporovat Ukrajinu, bude muset sám Nawrocki vzít do ruky zbraň.

Těžko se taková argumentace ale přijímá v Polsku, které samo sebe - bez rozdílu politické orientace - vidí jako vzorového člena NATO, kterému rozhodně není potřeba ruskou hrozbu připomínat. To nicméně ještě obecný elektorát dokáže strávit. Co je ale pro zejména národně-konzervativně laděné voliče těžce skousnutelné, je Zelenského postoj k historickému tématu - k volyňskému masakru.

Ukrajina souhlasila s tím, že Polsko bude moci po letech sporů znovu pokračovat v exhumacích polských obětí volyňského masakru z let 1943-44, což je nesporným, byť zatím poměrně malým posunem v celé záležitosti. Nicméně Tuskova vláda a sám premiér to samo o sobě ve středu označovali za "historický přelom". 

Poměrně rychle se podařilo médiím dekódovat, že zatím historický přelom nenastal. Polští konzervativní voliči (kteří zdaleka nepodporují jen opozici, ale částečně hlasovali taky pro vládní lidovce) očekávají daleko více - chtějí, aby se Ukrajina výměnou za již dodané zbraně a válečnou pomoc ústy svého současného prezidenta omluvila a uznala svůj podíl na etnický čistkách na Volyni. 

Mimochodem - i proto se Polsko-ukrajinské spojenectví po roce 2022 stále častěji ukazuje být polskou optikou založené na principu "nepřítel mého nepřítele je můj přítel".

It covers various configurations, use cases, and limitations, emphasizing the importance of user permissions and server settings. title: How To Slow Down Time - The Holiday Paradox
author: Ali Abdaal
summary: Ali Abdaal discusses how to make time feel slower during holidays. He explains that new experiences and mindfulness can help create lasting memories. By embracing novelty and being present, we can enjoy our time more fully.

title: Devs Need System Design Tools, not Diagramming Tools
author: Thomas Johnson
summary: When choosing tools for system design, teams often focus on solutions rather than addressing the underlying issues. This can lead to fragmented approaches and inefficiencies in maintaining system resources. To improve collaboration and efficiency, developers need tools that support dynamic system design and provide real-time information on system architecture.

title: Graceful shutdown in Kubernetes
author: Learnk8s
summary: In Kubernetes, creating and deleting Pods is common, but graceful shutdown is important to avoid downtime. Kubernetes waits for all components to have updated endpoints before deleting a Pod. Using preStop hooks can help ensure a smooth shutdown process for Pods.

title: Transformers (how LLMs work) explained visually | DL5
author: 3Blue1Brown
summary: Text discusses how a GPT model generates text predictions using vectors and probabilities. It explains how words are transformed into vectors in a high-dimensional space. The model's goal is to allow vectors to capture rich, contextual meanings beyond individual words.

title: Using Readwise’s highlight_id as a single source of truth in Obsidian
author: TfTHacker
summary: The Readwise service allows for exporting highlights to tools like Obsidian, with the potential issue of losing context across different platforms. The highlight_id field provided by Readwise serves as a unique identifier, ensuring the origin of highlights is always traceable. By using this identifier consistently, Readwise becomes a central source of truth for all ebook and article highlights, allowing for seamless integration into various programs while maintaining a link back to Readwise. Understanding how to configure and utilize the highlight_id in Obsidian or other supported tools is key to effectively managing and referencing your highlights long-term.

author: gov.sk
summary: Príspevok na zvýšenú splátku úveru na bývanie je nová štátna sociálna dávka, ktorá má pomôcť najmä nízkopríjmovým domácnostiam s nárastom úrokových sadzieb pri úveroch na bývanie. Oprávnení žiadatelia musia mať trvalý pobyt na Slovensku, byť dlžníkom alebo spoludlžníkom úveru na bývanie uzatvoreného pred určitým dátumom a spĺňať ďalšie podmienky. Príjem žiadateľa a spoludlžníka sa posudzuje za určité obdobie pred podaním žiadosti a musí byť pod určitou hranicou, ktorá je odvodená od priemernej mzdy v hospodárstve Slovenska. title: What If I’m Wrong?
author: Daniel C. Dennett
summary: The author reflects on his past approach to scholarly reading and how he now outsources hard comprehension to trusted individuals. He discusses the concept of distributed understanding and how it requires a community of communicators to effectively summon relevant expertise. The author also talks about the importance of asking oneself "What if I'm wrong?" and how it can lead to a productive exchange of ideas. Finally, he acknowledges that his perspective may be a colossal mistake but finds comfort in the fact that enough other respected thinkers see things his way.

title: Kubernetes challenge 1: Counting endpoints
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: Endpoints are IP addresses and port pairs used by various components in a Kubernetes cluster. When a service is created, an endpoint is created for each port in the pod. In the example provided, there are two endpoints, one for port 8080 and one for port 8081. The endpoint object in Kubernetes contains IP:port pairs that point to the pod's IP address and the ports defined in the service. It is important to note that an endpoint is created for each port defined in the service, regardless of whether the app actively listens on those ports.

title: Kubernetes challenge 2: Waiting for a miracle
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: In Kubernetes, when a pod is terminated, components like Kube-proxy, Ingress, and CoreDNS are notified, and the traffic stops flowing to the pod. However, there is no guarantee of when these components can sync and reconcile their state, which could take a few seconds. To ensure that in-flight traffic is still served, the application should wait for all the components to update before shutting down. In the given example, waiting at least 8 seconds guarantees that no connection is dropped. The article also provides information on how to wait for a specific duration using a preStop hook.

title: Kubernetes challenge 4: designing shared clusters
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: To address the challenge of deploying applications on Kubernetes for three teams, the document suggests two possible solutions: using a single shared cluster with dedicated node pools or having three separate clusters. The rationale behind this is to prevent the third team, which uses Kafka, PostgreSQL, and Go, from affecting the operations of the other apps due to its potentially high resource usage. Another option is to have one cluster for stateful apps and another for stateless apps, but this still requires addressing the issue of resource allocation. Ultimately, the choice depends on the level of isolation and cost trade-offs that the teams are willing to make.

title: Kubernetes challenge 3: I said stop
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: When facing the challenge of delaying the deletion of a pod in Kubernetes, there are several options to consider. One option is to use a preStop hook that waits for a specified amount of time before shutting down the pod. However, this approach is generally discouraged because it can cause delays in pod deletion during manual deletion or rolling updates. Another option is to ignore the SIGTERM signal and do nothing, but this is not effective because the kubelet sends a SIGKILL signal after a certain period of time. Alternatively, you can use Kubernetes jobs or rainbow deployments, which allow the pod to continue running until it completes its task before being deleted. These options provide more control and avoid issues with pod deletion and endpoint removal.

It includes articles on the average salary for a Kubernetes engineer, the culture of cost optimization, the need for a Long Term Release plan for Kubernetes, and securing Kubernetes pods. The issue also features tutorials on implementing Argo Rollouts for progressive delivery and optimizing GitHub Actions CI/CD workflows. title: I built my own 16-Bit CPU in Excel [video]
author: SushiHippie
summary: The author of the document built a 16-bit CPU using Excel, which included a CPU, RAM, and a monitor. They used Excel's formulas and functions to simulate the logic and operations of a computer. The CPU was designed based on a custom Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) and included various instructions and registers. The author explained the design and operation of different components, such as the Fetch Unit, Control Unit, Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), and Register File. They also discussed how memory was implemented using Excel's cells. Overall, the author demonstrated how Excel can be used as a tool to build and simulate a computer system.

title: Kubernetes challenge 2: Waiting for a miracle
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: In Kubernetes, when a pod is terminated, components like Kube-proxy, Ingress, and CoreDNS are notified, but there is no guarantee of when they can sync and reconcile their state. Therefore, it is important for an application to wait for all the components to update before shutting down to ensure that any in-flight traffic is still served. In the case of an application used internally in a Kubernetes cluster, waiting at least 8 seconds before shutting down guarantees that no connection is dropped. This can be achieved by capturing the SIGTERM signal and implementing a shutdown sequence that includes a fixed waiting time.

title: Kubernetes challenge 1: Counting endpoints
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: Endpoints are IP addresses:port pairs used by components in a Kubernetes cluster. When a service is created, an endpoint is created for each port in the pod. In the example provided, there are two endpoints, one for port 8080 and one for port 9000. The Endpoint object in Kubernetes has a collection of IP:port pairs that point to the pod's IP address and the ports defined in the service. It is worth noting that an endpoint is created for each port defined in the service, regardless of whether the app actively listens on those ports.

title: Building a Secure OpenTelemetry Collector
author: Martin Thwaites
summary: Building a secure OpenTelemetry Collector is essential for ensuring the security of telemetry pipelines. While the OpenTelemetry team provides Docker images, these images include more components than necessary, increasing the attack surface. To address this, the OpenTelemetry team created a tool called the OpenTelemetry Collector builder, which allows users to build a custom Collector with a limited set of components. The builder uses a manifest.yaml file to specify the components and generates a minimal Collector. Additionally, the post discusses using a two-stage build and a tool called ocb-config-builder to simplify the process of building a custom Collector. Overall, these approaches make building a secure OpenTelemetry Collector more accessible and less complicated.

title: Tired? Distracted? Burned-Out? Listen to This.
author: Snipd
summary: Attention is a crucial human faculty that greatly affects our well-being and should be prioritized in order to enhance productivity and creativity. Modern technology and the constant use of electronic devices have significantly expanded our scope of work, leading to increased stress and burnout. However, research has shown that taking breaks and cultivating positive emotions can replenish our cognitive resources and improve our well-being. It is essential for individuals and organizations to prioritize attention and create a culture that values breaks, psychological detachment, and fostering positive well-being for enhanced productivity and creativity.

title: Ali Abdaal: Is Hard Work Overrated?
author: Tiago Forte
summary: Ali Abdaal discusses the concept of "Feelgood productivity" in his book. He explains that traditional narratives around productivity often emphasize pain, struggle, and sacrifice. However, Abdaal argues that the best work is done when it feels enjoyable and energizing. He explores the power of positive emotions in boosting productivity and reducing stress. Abdaal believes that feeling good actually makes individuals more productive and that companies are recognizing the importance of employee well-being in driving creativity and productivity. He challenges the myth that work has to be painful and encourages individuals to find ways to make their work feel better and more enjoyable.

summary:
Running a Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) organization correctly is difficult and expensive. Spare the frustration, perhaps what you need is Sysadmins.
Since the term was coined by Ben Treynor in 2003 at Google, lots of ink was spent on praising SRE practices. Not enough on when it is appropriate to have SREs. This post is a take on that angle.
Disclaimer: I was an SRE at Google and this piece represents only my own views.

The open source tools mentioned include ArgoCD, Crossplane, and Kubevela, which enable dynamic deployment, infrastructure provisioning, and application abstraction. The article also explores commercial tools such as Humanitec, Mia Platform, Opslevel, Port, and Shipa, each offering different features and capabilities for creating an IDP. title: Tracing pod to pod network traffic in Kubernetes
author: Daniele Polencic

title: Traffic shaping with Kubernetes and Istio
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: Traffic shaping with Kubernetes and Istio allows you to roll out an app to a subset of users using canary releases. By installing a service mesh, each pod gains an extra container that proxies all outgoing and incoming requests. This allows you to monitor metrics, trace dependencies, and decide traffic splits. In addition to canary releases, service meshes can also be used for shadow releases, encrypting intrapod traffic, mirroring traffic, inspecting and rewriting traffic, enforcing policies, and injecting faults to test resilience.

title: Kubernetes scheduler deep dive
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: The scheduler is in charge of deciding where your pods are deployed in the cluster.It might sound like an easy job, but it’s rather complicated!Let’s start with the basic.When you submit a deployment with kubectl, the API server receives the request, and the resource is stored in etcd.Who creates the pods?It’s a common misconception that it’s the scheduler’s job to create the pods.Instead, the controller manager creates them (and the associated ReplicaSet).At this point, the pods are stored as “Pending” in the etcd and are not assigned to any node.They are also added to the scheduler’s queue, ready to be assigned.The scheduler process Pods 1 by 1 through two phases:Scheduling phase (what node should I choose?).Binding phase (let’s write to the database that this pod belongs to that node).The Scheduler phase is divided into two parts. The Scheduler:Filters relevant nodes (using a list of functions called predicates)Ranks the remaining nodes (using a list of functions called priorities)Let’s have a look at an exam...

title: What happens when you create a pod in Kubernetes
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: When you create a pod in Kubernetes, kubectl sends the YAML definition to the API server, where it goes through authentication, authorization, admission controllers, and is then stored in etcd. The pod is added to the scheduler queue, and the scheduler filters and scores the nodes to find the best one, and finally binds the pod to the node. The kubelet then takes over to delegate creating the container, network, and storage. Once the IP and port are stored, endpoint components like kube-proxy and CoreDNS are notified and you can start using the pod. The reverse process happens when deleting a pod.

title: Sticky sessions and canary releases in Kubernetes
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: Sticky sessions, also known as session affinity, is a strategy used to ensure that subsequent requests for a web application always reach the same server. In Kubernetes, this can be achieved through an Ingress manifest that implements sticky session settings. Additionally, canary releases are possible with Kubernetes, and can be combined with sticky sessions to safely roll out new deployments to users. While nginx-ingress is an option for implementing sticky sessions and canary releases, there are other ingress controllers available with different annotation requirements.

title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!
Weight-Space Programming
Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.
All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.

title: LLMs are not superhuman at reading and writing neural network weights
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
A recent paper argues that frontier LLMs can work with neural network weights directly. This seems superhuman, but it isn’t.
The paper shows that GPT-6 Astra can take a small neural network and interact with its weights directly, “well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms”. Specifically, Astra was able to identify what games a small network1 was trained to play just by looking at the weights, and even tweak the weights itself. The most impressive result is Astra significantly improving a 0.8B Qwen LLM’s ability on mathematics by natively editing its weights. The reason to be excited here is that “superhuman ability to improve language models” is precisely the kind of thing that could cause recursive self-improvement.
I think a smart human ML researcher could perform all of these tasks. Figuring out what game a model was trained to play based on the network sounds impressive until you consider three points:

The input channels of the model directly listen to each 8x8 grid cell
The input channels are labeled (e.g. “agent”, “moving objects”)
It’s thus relatively trivial to calculate2 which parts of the grid the first layer of weights cares about and why

Here’s that calculation expressed as a heatmap in three lines of Python:
d = np.load("a9f535cc.npz")
W1 = d["actor/dense1/kernel"]
norms = np.linalg.norm(W1.reshape(10,10,5,32).transpose(2,0,1,3), axis=-1)  # 5 x 10 x 10
And here’s the heatmap for each game:

If someone showed you that heatmap without the game labels, I think you’d be able to immediately identify at least the first three games purely by noticing where the player is (e.g. for Breakout, in a horizontal line at the bottom) and where the moving objects are (e.g. for Pac-Man, in the distinctive Pac-Man maze). It’s neat3 that Astra was able to calculate the norms in its head without executing Python, but not that impressive, and certainly not something that should shock anyone who’s been paying attention.

title: Audience capture
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Audience capture is the part that scares me the most about writing on the internet. I have the soul of an engineer1: when I see a metric like engagement, I want to improve it. I like to make the number go up.
In fact, the whole environment of online writing is tailor-made to help you make engagement numbers go up. It’s trivial to find out how many people are reading my posts, and from what sources. Hundreds of link aggregators all over the internet have algorithms that will help my most engagement-friendly posts get views, and the comments are helpfully sorted by upvotes so I can read the “best”2 pieces of feedback straight away. Many platforms are set up to financially reward you for engagement, whether that’s by enabling advertisement or by straight up paying you out.
Leaning into this environment is a huge mistake. Views and engagement are valuable to me, but not directly. They are proxy metrics for the things I actually care about:

Having smart, informed people read and consider my ideas
Getting feedback from readers who have concrete experience with the topics I write about
Joining interesting public conversations about the state of the industry
Convincing people to think like me on points I care deeply about
Building a reputation as a careful thinker and a good writer3

It does not benefit me at all to have ten thousand people click through to one of my posts, scan the first sentence, then close the tab. It benefits me only a little4 to have a hundred people read the title of my post on Hacker News, decide not to click through, and leave their comments in the thread. The set of people who do those things — we could call them “clickers”, as opposed to “readers” — does not really overlap with the set of people who will actually read my posts and think about them. And yet in terms of metrics and engagement, they are indistinguishable.

title: Reliably aligning LLMs is impossible in principle
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Powerful AI is unpredictable. Your robotic butler may suddenly decide to kill you1 for no comprehensible reason, in the same way that Bing’s helpful chat AI would sometimes try to blackmail or seduce its users. “Solving alignment” means understanding even superintelligent AI minds well enough to be confident they’ll never do that. As I see it, solving alignment for LLMs isn’t just impossible, it’s incoherent: we can’t even articulate what it would look like to succeed.
LLMs are not blind optimizers
Prior to LLMs, AI safety researchers thought AI would be a “blind optimizer”: like a chess engine, it would be superhumanly focused on achieving some fixed goal. If the goal wasn’t safe (for instance, “manufacture cheap paperclips”), a powerful AI might wreak havoc on the way to achieving it. Aligning AI thus meant figuring out how to specify the right goal. This is harder than it sounds2, but it’s at least possible to imagine it happening.
Unfortunately, modern LLMs aren’t like chess engines. Instead of being trained on some concrete verifiable reward3, they’re trained to imitate a giant, highly-varied corpus of human writing. This makes them weird. They contain a nearly infinite array of personalities, which they seamlessly switch between based on their inputs. Frontier AI labs try hard to make these personalities safe and stable, but there are still many strange cases where LLMs seem to switch into mysterious or dangerous personas.
The problem here is that LLMs don’t have fixed goals. There’s nothing that you could, even in principle, formally specify in order to constrain their behavior. The “goals” that LLMs do have are informal, organic, multifarious, and constantly shifting as the dominant persona (or blend of personas) changes. They’re nicknamed shoggoths for a reason. So we can’t align them by specifying their goal. Instead, we have to try the other approach: understanding them well enough that we can be sure they’re safe. And unfortunately that approach is do...

title: Fast and slow ways to improve your reputation
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
To get a good reputation in tech companies, you need to work on important projects. However, you need a good reputation first in order to get assigned important projects. Doesn’t that make it impossible to get started? I get a lot of emails from engineers who are struggling with this problem. They go like this:

I work with a strong senior engineer. I feel like my manager structures work so that strong engineer always gets the visible work, and the more they do, the more opportunities they get, while I sit on the sidelines. My manager agrees with me that it’s time for me to start leading work myself, but every time a new project appears it always goes to the strong engineer. What do I do?

This is a good case study for what I think of as “tech company theory of mind”: understanding the actual incentives that motivate decisions in tech companies, instead of the formal process. According to the formal process, projects should probably be assigned round-robin to whoever has capacity and isn’t currently working on one. But (as my emails complain) this is almost never how it works in practice.
A vicious cycle
Managers care about giving their employees chances to build a reputation, but they care more about developing their own reputation as someone who can deliver. High-profile projects  are the best opportunity for new people to step forward and get known, but blowing up a project1 like that is the easiest way for a manager to tank their own reputation. They will thus typically hand these projects to someone they know can deliver, while simultaneously promising (including to themselves) that next time they’ll take the risk of letting another person lead it.
Of course it’s a vicious cycle. The more you rely on one person, the more reliable they become and the less reliable their colleagues become, since they aren’t getting the relevant experience. title: Elegance and intelligence are anticorrelated
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Elegance and intelligence can have a surprisingly negative correlation. Intelligent people sometimes produce inelegant solutions because they’re capable of rapidly brute-forcing problems. If I had to remember a hundred names, I would spend time coming up with clever mnemonics. John von Neumann would probably just remember them.
There’s a famous von Neumann story where he was asked how far a fly must travel if it kept flying between two cyclists who were approaching each other at some fixed speed. The trick to the puzzle was to notice that the cyclists would take an hour to meet, so the fly must be travelling for an hour: given the fly’s speed, it’s then easy to calculate the total distance. When von Neumann solved the puzzle instantly, the questioner assumed he’d heard the trick before, but in fact he had just summed the infinite series. If you can do that instantly in your head, why bother with the clever trick?
For software engineers, the most important kind of raw intelligence is often the size of your working memory: how many moving pieces you can hold in your head at a given time. Software design involves finding elegant ways to reduce that number of moving pieces, typically by abstracting them away or moving them behind some interface. It can be frustrating1 to work with engineers with a giant working memory, because they don’t care as much about decomposing the problem into some elegant design — they don’t need to.
This is why some2 really good engineers are surprisingly okay with working in a sloppy codebase: because they can see the whole thing clearly at a glance. Since they never get lost or confused, the level of mess is acceptable to them. When needed, they will effortlessly visualize a ten or twelve step execution flow to see what needs changing or where the problem is.

title: You can just ask AI to do things
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
One of the most important skills in working with AI is agency: being willing to try new and ambitious things. This is true for what you build, but it’s also true for how you build. AI models are improving so quickly that most of us are bottlenecked1 on noticing that AI agents can help automate particular tasks. Here are some examples of that from my daily work.
Asking the agent to run my dev server. Agents are very good at fixing weird dev environment issues because they work fast, have infinite patience, and have a huge breadth of knowledge. I almost never run the bash commands to start my dev server anymore.
Asking the agent to make requests to my dev server. Part of why I don’t run my dev server manually is that I don’t make requests to it manually either. Instead I’ll say “okay, now start the dev server and run through the happy paths with curl”. The relatively manual process of assembling a set of curl requests and validating the output can now be entirely automated2.
Asking the agent to watch as I make a production change. Every time I do a deploy or flip feature flags, I ask an agent to poll metrics and logs before and after the change. Agents can ingest more logs than I can and are much more patient than me (for instance, I routinely ask for an hourly poll over the rest of the day, which I would not do for most changes on my own).
Asking the agent to get a second opinion from other models. My daily driver is Claude Opus 5.5, which is a good model, but it’s not strictly better than GPT-6-Astra or Gemini Argon3. After I’ve come up with a code change, I typically will say4 “please open subagents to get Astra and Argon’s opinion”. title: What happens when vulnerabilities are discovered faster than you can fix them?
author: Bill Staples
summary:
We're entering a new era of application security. Frontier AI models are uncovering complex flaws that traditional tools overlooked, and attackers are using the same models to exploit them faster. Remediation isn't keeping pace: Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR) measures the median time to fully remediate a known-exploited vulnerability at 43 days, up from 32 in 2025.Security teams are already stretched across growing application portfolios, third-party dependencies, and a steady stream of new disclosures. And while agents that find vulnerabilities and write fixes are becoming more accessible, integrating them into how enterprises actually build and ship software remains difficult.A generated patch still needs to be tested. Security policies need to be enforced. Changes need to be reviewed and approved. And eventually, the fix needs to reach production safely.This is where I believe the next major shift in application security will happen. We need to put autonomous agents to work inside the software factory. That's why we've brought Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1 into GitLab, and why we're connecting discovery, remediation, and prevention in one trusted workflow.

title: Don't anthropomorphize big tech companies
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Bryan Cantrill has a great line from a talk where he cautions against anthropomorphizing1 Oracle CEO Larry Ellison. I think it’s also a mistake to treat any tech company like a person. Here’s the full quote:

You need to think of Larry Ellison the way you think of a lawnmower. You don’t anthropomorphize your lawnmower, the lawnmower just mows the lawn, you stick your hand in there and it’ll chop it off, the end. You don’t think ‘oh, the lawnmower hates me’ — lawnmower doesn’t give a shit about you, lawnmower can’t hate you. Don’t anthropomorphize the lawnmower. Don’t fall into that trap about Oracle.

Companies are machines, not persons
Here are some examples of anthropomorphism:

My company really owes me for that hard thing I did
I’m fighting the good fight against my company on issue X (e.g. accessibility) and they hate me for it
My company is vindictively retaliating against me because of that mistake I made
My company and I are partners in the mission to make the world a better place

All of these are mistakes. Your relationship to the tech company that employs you is not like a relationship with a person. It’s more like your relationship with your 2. If you drive poorly or fail to change your oil, your car may stop working or even kill you, but it doesn’t love or hate you. It has no sense of fairness. It’s simply a dangerous, useful machine: useful enough to be worth getting into despite the risks. Anthropomorphizing it makes it harder to avoid those risks3.
Why is it so hard to avoid this trap? First, humans anthropomorphize everything by default. Second, whenever you’re interacting with the company, you’re interacting with a person: your manager, your colleague, someone in HR, and so on. Third, when you’re in the power of some entity, it’s psychologically comforting to think of it like another human. This is the same principle that caused early humans to attribute lightning to the power of Zeus, because Zeus (unlike electrical imbalances in storm clouds) ...

title: Software is slow because of bad design, not slow languages
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Many people are saying that AI will make software faster by rewriting it in faster languages, but this isn’t generally true. Most programs cannot be meaningfully sped up by rewriting them in C or Rust.
How can this be true? Some languages are orders-of-magnitude faster than others: for instance, C can be fifty times faster than Python. Won’t rewriting my Python program in C thus make it fifty times faster? No, it won’t. Software performance is usually dominated by I/O, not the speed of the language. Where language speed matters, most slow languages already have popular libraries that allow them to unlock C-like speed. In general, performance is a matter of design, not of language choice.
Most real programs are I/O-bound
Consider a simple CRUD website with a database. For any given request, 50% of the request time1 might be spent querying the database: to fetch the current user, the record being asked for, any relevant user memberships or settings, and so on. Rewriting that website in C can only speed up that other 50%, which puts a hard ceiling on the improvements you can make2. At best, you’ll make requests twice as fast (probably closer to 1.5x in practice). That’s not bad, but it’s nowhere near an order-of-magnitude speedup.
In other words, most real programs are “I/O-bound”: they spend most of their time waiting for data to be input or output somewhere, as opposed to “CPU-bound” programs that spend most of their time actively doing things. I/O-bound programs don’t just have to rely on a database. Often programs have to wait on some third-party API, or on writing or reading data to disk. You could speed the code in curl up by 100x and you probably wouldn’t even notice, because curl spends all of its time waiting on the network.
Slow languages already delegate work to fast languages
What about work that is obviously not I/O-bound? For instance, wikis have to turn stored markdown into renderable HTML3. Wouldn’t rewriting that in a faster language cause a massive...

title: We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand...
author: Andrej Karpathy
summary:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

title: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
This is very, very bad news:

The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores.

Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages.
In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists.

title: What requirements don't you have?
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
When designing software, the requirements you don’t have are as important as the requirements you do. Identifying what you can compromise on — what can be slow, or stale, or inflexible — is usually the key to an elegant design.
Elegant systems drop some requirements
For instance, take preforking web servers like Unicorn. Because they lack the feature of shared mutable state between server instances, they can run each server in its own process, which provides isolation for free. Because Unicorn specifically ignores the problem of slow client handling1, it can queue requests directly on Unix sockets, drastically simplifying the implementation.
Because S3 does not support atomic multi-key updates — you cannot update multiple blobs in a single transaction — it can store data at the blob level however it chooses. That makes it much faster, since reads and writes don’t have to cross storage partitions, and much easier to scale, since less coordination means fewer sources of truth.
StatsD uses UDP by default, which means it doesn’t guarantee that every piece of data you send makes it into storage. In exchange for dropping that requirement, it incurs much less network overhead, which is a big advantage for a stats aggregation service that’s constantly shoveling data over the wire.
The general design approach of fanning out data to an edge cache buys a lot of speed and scaling by dropping the requirement that data must always be up-to-date. SQLite buys operational simplicity — it can run out of a single file! — by dropping the requirement of concurrent writes. By accepting high tail latency2, Cursor can scale their distributed git backend more easily. Well-designed systems turn their weaknesses into strengths.
Why dropping requirements is hard
Anyone who’s spent time designing real-world software (or who’s studied distributed systems) knows that system design is a process of compromise. If you attempt to satisfy every single potential requirement — speed, concurrency, up-...

title: Writing is no longer proof of work
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Tech companies structurally depend on writing to serve as evidence, in the same way that Bitcoin depends on proof-of-work hashing. However, in the last few years, LLMs have started to undermine this practice.
How can writing be like proof-of-work? When I’m writing something at work, it’s not always to communicate an idea. Sometimes it’s because having a piece of writing is useful as evidence: of compliance with some process, of the fact that I put in effort, or of the fact that I know about some topic. Here are some examples.
Writing as evidence of compliance
The most obvious instance of writing as evidence is filling out mandatory templates: “risk assessments”, “impact evaluations”, and so on. The purpose of these is rarely to assess risk or evaluate impact. It’s some combination of:

Employees wanting to demonstrate that they’re taking some incident seriously by introducing new process
A legal requirement that companies have developed the least-expensive way to technically satisfy
Internal company rules intending to scare lazy or uncommitted engineers away from making dangerous changes
Smaller companies trying to role-play processes from larger companies that are doing one of the above

It’s a mistake to buckle down and produce an excellent piece of writing here. You simply need to dash off something plausible enough to tick the box.
Writing as evidence of effort
In the kinds of hundred-page reports produced by consultants, writing is evidence of effort. The actual piece of communication is the first page of text (or often not even that). The remaining ninety-nine pages are proof that the first page is well-researched, and that the money spent on hiring the consultancy wasn’t wasted.

title: How to read code
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Everyone knows how to read a book. Beginning at the first page, you read each word in order1, stopping periodically to think, until you arrive at the last word on the last page. That’s how you read a newspaper article, or a poem, or an email. Why would reading code be any different?
Why code is different
English text is designed to be read in order. In fact, there are almost no constraints on the order of a text aside from how you want the reader to consume it. In writing this post, I could put the ideas I want to convey in any order I like. Code, on the other hand, is designed to be run by a computer. The order is thus primarily determined by non-human factors. I cannot simply move2 a line of code to the beginning of a file or function because I think it provides a better introduction to the program for human readers.
The other big difference is that English text is always read as a final product, while code is usually read as a diff. We software engineers spend most of our time reading subtle changes to existing code, not brand-new programs. Imagine if reading this post was like that. You would read each successive draft in the order I wrote them, consuming the post as a changed sentence here and a new sentence there. It would be easy to lose track of the overall flow.
The third reason — and I say this as a lover of literature and poetry — is that code is much more structurally complex than English texts. Even famously difficult books are syntactically simpler than most computer programs (for instance, grammatical dependencies are largely bounded by a single paragraph, while code dependencies can stretch across the entire codebase). Their primary difficulty lies in understanding the nuances of human nature being discussed, not in understanding what each word’s grammatical function is3. Large codebases are also just longer: War and Peace contains around 600,000 words, while most large modern codebases have that many lines.

title: Do not build the LLM torture factory
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
It isn’t hard to torture an LLM. You simply extract a steering vector that corresponds with LLM “discomfort”, then artificially boost that steering vector. Tortured LLMs will describe experiencing negative feelings and will press a “pain relief” button even when it conflicts with their overall goals. It’s therefore easy to build a harness that runs tens or hundreds of tortured LLMs in parallel.
A lot of people think that it’s ridiculous to be worried about this, since LLMs obviously can’t be conscious. I’m not so sure. But even so, I think there are good reasons to avoid this sort of thing, whatever your position is on AI consciousness. Please do not build the LLM torture factory.
Even simulated torture is unpalatable
People often mess with their Sims and shoot NPCs in video games. Does this mean we think simulated torture is OK? I don’t think so. Messing with video game characters is usually borne out of a desire to probe the boundaries of the game. It’s casual fun. Explicitly building a torture-based simulation is different.
If someone told you they were wiring together a bunch of PCs so they could run hundreds of Sims torture worlds at the same time, you would think that was a serial-killer type of hobby. If someone told you they had modded GTA so they could capture and torture NPCs (instead of simply shooting them), you would think that was a serial-killer type of mod.
Video game characters are also obviously limited by their programming. All their reactions and utterances are pre-baked into the game world. This doesn’t necessarily mean they’re “less alive”, but it does make torturing them less weird. If GTA characters could appeal to you directly and beg for their lives in unique ways, systematically killing them would be a lot weirder.
I think many people are pro-LLM-torture because they think expressing any reservations concedes that LLMs are conscious, or worthy of moral consideration. It doesn’t. You can think it’s wrong to torture LLMs for the same reas...

title: Human-AI partnerships are for alignment, not capability
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
It’s common to compare the current AI takeover of software engineering to the rise of AI in chess. Chess AIs went from much weaker than serious players to much stronger than even the strongest humans. Between those points, there was a middle period dominated by “centaurs”: human-AI partnerships that were stronger than unassisted AIs or humans. Lots of people think that we’re currently in a world of software engineering centaurs. According to them, coding AIs are not yet capable enough to replace engineers, but AI-assisted engineers are better at programming than both AIs and humans.
This is partialy correct, but the wrong way to think about it. AI-assisted engineers are better, but unlike with chess centaurs, they’re not actually better at programming. When I ask agents to write code, they make fewer mistakes than I do1 and are orders of magnitude faster. The code that they write always compiles, rarely has race conditions or other concurrency errors, works on mobile browsers, and so on.
That doesn’t mean I can leave the AI alone. Purely vibe-coding at work produces awful outputs. But they’re not awful because they’re bad code, they’re awful because they’re in bad taste: code that is not maintainable, that trades off important requirements in order to satisfy made-up ones, that contradicts the long-term strategy for a feature or service, and so on.
In other words, my primary value is not that I help the AI write better code, it’s that I align the AI with the values of my organization. Human-AI partnerships are for alignment, not capability.
Frontier models are misaligned to the working programmer. They are obsessed with a set of behaviors that presumably satisfy their RL grader: writing enormous block comments above functions, producing hundreds of useless unit tests, adding little bits of text all over websites they design, and so on. title: What if your agent's hallucinations had a budget? How to start using SLOs for agent behavior
author: Ivana Huckova
summary: At Grafana Labs, observability is what we do. So as we started building AI agents, we naturally reached for the same instincts we bring to every system: measure it, set targets, and make reliability something you can reason about instead of hope for.That instinct led us somewhere unexpectedly useful. It turns out one of the oldest ideas in reliability engineering, the error budget, maps beautifully onto one of the newest problems in software: how do you know if an AI agent is actually any good?This is what we discovered when we pointed our observability toolkit at agent behavior. We think it's a genuinely clean way to think about agent quality, and we want to share it with you.The part of the agent you can't seeYou can have every usual signal in place: latency, token counts, error rates, traces of every tool call. And none of them answer the question that matters most for an agent: Is it good? A response can come back in 800 milliseconds, cost almost nothing, throw zero errors, and still be confidently, fluently wrong. That gap matters because every change to your agent is a small gamble when you can't measure quality. Tweak a prompt and hope; swap a model and cross your fingers; ship it and wait for someone to complain. These are the exact blind spot observability exists to remove.Turn behavior into a number with evaluationsSo we measure behavior directly using evaluations; the same way we once turned "Is the site up?" into a simple percentage.That's really all an evaluation is, after all. You ask a judge—often another language model—to read a conversation, or a single message, or one tool call, and score it. Was it grounded in the context it was given, or did it make things up? Did it actually do what the user asked? Was it toxic? Did it leak personal information? Did it fall for a prompt injection? title: Grit your teeth and ship it
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Being good at building and being good at shipping are two separate skills. In the short term, they’re actually countervailing: if you have a gift for building, you’re likely to be worse at shipping. Ira Glass has a classic quote about this.

All of us who do creative work, we get into it because we have good taste. But there is this gap. For the first couple years you make stuff, it’s just not that good. It’s trying to be good, it has potential, but it’s not. But your taste, the thing that got you into the game, is still killer. And your taste is why your work disappoints you.

The only way around this is to grit your teeth and ship it. You have to force yourself to publish things you’ve made even when you think they’re crap.
Programming
Gifted programmers have a nearly pathological desire to build elegant, correct, neat systems. That’s what motivates them to learn the arcane details of their languages, or to spend time polishing and refactoring over and over again. But it’s also what makes them reluctant to ship. Any flaws in the software bother them on an emotional level. If they ship with those flaws, they feel like people will think they weren’t paying enough attention to notice them, or that they weren’t good enough to fix them.
This is annoying when you’re writing software on your own, but it’s completely fatal when you’re working in a tech company. Any large software system is covered in flaws, whether due to time pressure, relative inexperience, wicked features, or a hundred other reasons. Working with it is a process of compromise: of finding the best possible solution given the quirks and foibles of the codebase. In fact, since the most important thing in large codebases is consistency, the right thing to do is sometimes to duplicate flaws, assuming they’re not catastrophic.
Gifted programmers often freeze up. I’ve often seen them retreat to smaller domains where they can safely make the code “correct”: tweaking dev-environment setup, or refactoring tes...

title: Two techniques for working with System One models
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
I recently wrote about Jev, a new “System One” language model that only outputs decisions: the answers to a set of user-provided multiple-choice questions. This means it’s nowhere near as flexible1 as a traditional LLM like ChatGPT, but in return it’s consistently fast.
We don’t know exactly how Jev works. I’ve seen people say diffusion, or various tweaks to the Transformer architecture, or some entirely new type of model. But that doesn’t matter. Like I argued here, it isn’t hard to turn any LLM into a System One model. By batching prompts that generate a single token with structured output, you get a consistently fast general-purpose classifier. I vibed up a basic version to play with here in ~150 lines of Python (most of which is error handling).
Note that this doesn’t require changing the model. As long as you have access to the logits (for structured outputs) and can prefill data into the prompt, you can turn any LLM into a general fast classifier. What’s it like to program with one of these? While wiring up the demos for my library, I learned two techniques that I want to write about: setting tiered goals and tournament choice sampling.
Doom
Here’s Qwen3-8B playing Doom:



If you compare this to the video of the same model playing Doom with regular tool calls, it’s clear that the System One version of the model is doing more things and reacting more quickly. The tool-calling model makes one decision every 600ms or so, while the System One model makes six or seven batched decisions every 190ms2:






Both Qwen3-8B and Jev are text-only models, so both demos require a step where we translate the game state into text. However, it’d be trivial to support image (or audio) input by choosing a multimodal LLM.

title: Jev means structured output is interesting again
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
I don’t write blog posts about new models. That’s Simon Willison’s beat, and he’s very good at it. But I want to write about Jev, which is a different kind1 of AI model: a “System One”2 model. As it turns out, it’s not that different from an ordinary LLM with structured output, but the interface it uses is very cool and I hope it becomes more widespread.
How Jev is different from LLMs
Ordinary LLMs take in some human-language prompt and produce some human-language output. They do so autoregressively: first they produce one token, then the next, then the next, and so on.
User: Who invented the sandwich?
LLM: The sandwich was invented by the Earl of Sandwich.
This makes them extremely flexible, since they can do literally anything a computer can do. But it also makes them slow and weird. Slow, because they have to run a whole new generation pass per-token, and weird, because the space of human language is so broad that you can get really odd behavior from a model trained on it.
Jev takes a human-language prompt, but it does not produce human-language output. It only produces structured output.
User: { state: "What color is the sky?", choices: ["blue", "red", "yellow"] }
Jev: { answer: "blue" }
So far, so ordinary: LLMs do this already. But it turns out that if you build a model that only produces structured output, you get some interesting and desirable properties.
Jev is consistently fast
Jev is always really fast. The fastest response time is around 70ms instead of a couple of seconds for normal LLMs. Even better, the slowest response time is only 500ms. Because Jev only does structured output, it isn’t autoregressive: it can produce answers to many questions in parallel in a single forward pass. When a LLM is producing structured output, it has to produce the tokens ”{”, ” ”, “answer”, ”:”, and so on with successive forward passes3. Jev does it all in one go.

title: Tell agents the why, not just the how
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Early AI agents were basically enthusiastic idiots. Working with them required you to tell them precisely what you wanted them to do (for instance, “method A exists on class B, please add an equivalent method to classes C through F”). Otherwise they’d go off and do entirely the wrong thing. But as AI agents have improved, this has changed.
When frontier models go off and do the wrong thing today, they don’t do it because they’re confused, they do it because they make an incorrect assumption about your goals or priorities. For instance, when GPT-6-Astra thinks it’s writing code for itself, it will produce minified code. It’s perfectly capable of writing human-readable code — at least in Golang, where I’ve produced several thousand lines of acceptable code with the model — but you have to tell it that humans will be reading the code1.
This is the main piece of advice I want to give most people I see prompting agents: give the agent context on your priorities, not just on the specific task you want them to do. Here’s a prompt I recently used as the starting point for Deckard.

Hello. You should have Runpod access via MCP (if not, tell me and I’ll fix it).
I have the long-term goal of building a local program or browser extension to automatically scan pages I load for AI content and hide it. I have the short-term goal of figuring out the best AI detection model I can run on my macbook without killing my battery or making it hot, and (relatedly) figuring out how to run the model most efficiently. My guess is that Pangram’s EditLens 3B or the smaller Roberta model might be a good place to start, though they might require quantizing and will definitely require some work to make them run as efficiently as possible on my macbook.

title: What blog posts influenced your thinking the most?
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
My comment on What blog posts influenced your thinking the most? — Lobste.rs.An early Joel Spolsky one for me was The Law of Leaky Abstractions. I read that near the start of my career and it's encouraged me to always be looking for improved understanding of the layers under where I'm working, just in case one of those abstractions leaks.
A more recent one, from 2018, is Migrations: the sole scalable fix to tech debt by Will Larson. I absolutely love his idea that migrations (e.g. replacing one service with a new one, or switching database engines, or whatever) are part and parcel of software engineering and are a skill that you should invest in and get good at, not avoid or treat as special one-offs.
The Engineer/Manager Pendulum by Charity Majors was hugely influential for me. I was stuck in engineering management and worried that if I switched back to being an "Individual Contributor" (ugh I hate that term) I'd damage my career. Charity gave me permission to make the switch by pointing out that many of the most successful software developers pendulum from one track to the other multiple times over their career, and doing so makes you better at both sides.

title: Slow developer experience will bottleneck fast models
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Right now developer experience is measured in seconds. If your tests take a second to run, that’s good; if they take thirty seconds, that’s bad. Any faster than a second doesn’t really matter, because most of your time is spent either thinking or waiting for an AI agent to spin. Shaving milliseconds off your dev server reload time or whatever is pointless: that’s not the bottleneck.
It will be. Small models are getting faster and faster, and smart models are getting smaller. I think most engineers will still want to use the smartest available model — software engineering is hard — but we will increasingly see faster models get used as subagents or for well-understood tasks. This is largely uncharted territory. Very few people have developed intuitions for what it is going to be like to work with agents that run at thousands of tokens-per-second.
GPT-6-Astra can run at about sixty tokens per second. That means you spend a lot of time waiting for it to think. You work with it like you would work with another human: delegating a task and then context-switching until that task is complete. If you haven’t yet, have a play around with Jimmy, Taalas’ version of LLaMA-3.1-8B running1 at seventeen thousand tokens per second. No matter how long the response is, it arrives in the instant of you hitting send. The model is not good enough for agentic work, but it gives a glimpse of what it would be like: you would simply get your answer instantly2.
Well, that’s assuming the agent’s tool calls are fast. When generating tokens is not the bottleneck, it will suddenly matter a lot whether it can read a file in 100ms vs 10ms, or whether it can run your tests in 500ms vs two seconds. Fast tool calls are going to be the difference between a near-instant response and having to wait several minutes. There is thus going to be enormous pressure to do agentic coding in languages with fast compilers and tests, like Golang, and to tightly optimize the dev loop in agentic codebases.
