This leadership style contrasts with traditional models by focusing on empathy, listening, and community building. While it has faced criticisms regarding its historical implications and lack of empirical support, many aspects of servant leadership can still positively influence organizations.

title: Advantages of incompetent management
author: yosefk.com
summary: Incompetent management can sometimes lead to unexpected benefits, like increased efficiency, because employees are free to pursue their interests without strict goals. Competent management often creates bureaucracy and pressure that stifle creativity and spontaneity, making it harder to innovate. Embracing a more relaxed approach can allow motivated individuals to thrive and adapt more easily to changes.

title: Categories of leadership on technical teams
author: Jose Luis Ricon
summary: The author discusses how to structure leadership within technical teams by categorizing responsibilities into overall direction, people management, and project management. Each category plays a crucial role in ensuring teams work effectively towards their goals, with clear communication and collaboration among leaders. The text also highlights that while these roles can overlap, understanding their distinctions helps new managers navigate their responsibilities better.

title: Perfectionism - one of the biggest productivity killers in the engineering industry
author: Gregor Ojstersek
summary: Perfectionism can significantly harm productivity in the engineering industry. It often leads to stress and burnout because projects become endless "work in progress." The article aims to share mistakes to help others avoid these pitfalls.

title: Accountability sinks
author: Mandy Brown
summary: Dan Davies argues that organizations create "accountability sinks" that hide the consequences of decisions, making it hard to hold anyone accountable. This occurs when there is a disconnect between those affected by a decision and those who make it. To be truly accountable, one must have the power to change decisions and understand how they came to be.

title: Learning to learn
author: Kevin Li
summary: Kevin Li conducts interviews to find the right fit for startups and values open-ended questions that reveal a candidate's unique insights. He emphasizes the importance of knowing what to learn and suggests a structured approach to becoming an expert. Learning efficiently can save time, as being more effective in fewer hours yields better results.

title: Phippy and Friends
author: Cloud Native Computing Foundation
summary: Phippy is a simple PHP app, trying to find a home with friends in a cloud native world. Are you a maintainer on a graduated project? Do you want to help others better understand the concepts of cloud…

title: ObservabilityCON 2024: On-demand sessions available now!
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: ObservabilityCON 2024 sessions are now available on-demand for those who missed the event in New York. Over a dozen videos cover the latest updates from Grafana Labs and insights from industry experts. You can also look forward to in-person learning opportunities with ObservabilityCON on the Road events coming soon.

title: What is zero trust authorization?
author: Jessie
summary: Zero trust authorization (ZTA) is a modern security approach that requires verification for every user and device, regardless of their location. It focuses on minimizing access permissions, assuming breaches are likely, and continuously monitoring for threats. This method improves security by providing better control and visibility while adapting to the challenges of cloud computing and remote work.

title: Grafana 11.3 release: Scenes-powered dashboards, visualization and panel updates, and more
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: Grafana 11.3 has been released with new Scenes-powered dashboards and improved visualization features. Users can now trigger API calls from dashboard elements and explore logs without complex queries. The update also includes enhanced alerting capabilities and simplified user access management.

title: From multi-line queries to no-code investigations: meeting Grafana users where they are
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: Grafana has introduced new Explore apps that make it easier for users of all skill levels to analyze telemetry data without needing to write complex queries. These apps provide a user-friendly, no-code experience for exploring metrics, logs, traces, and profiles. This approach allows both beginners and experienced developers to quickly gain insights into their software systems.

title: Daniele Polencic’s Post
author: Daniele Polencic
summary: Daniele Polencic has created 20 Kubernetes challenges since January 2024, based on questions from his courses and personal experiences. These challenges can help improve your Kubernetes knowledge and prepare for job interviews. He invites others to share their challenges or issues for potential future questions.

title: Key Prometheus concepts every Grafana user should know
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: Prometheus is a powerful monitoring framework, not just a time series database, offering features like metric scraping, querying, and alerting. The book "Prometheus Up & Running" reveals its full potential, especially for Grafana users, by explaining how to better manage and visualize metrics. Understanding Prometheus's capabilities, including PromQL and recording rules, can significantly enhance your observability practices.

title: How to use Prometheus to efficiently detect anomalies at scale
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: Grafana Labs has developed an anomaly detection framework using PromQL to help quickly identify and resolve incidents. This framework is designed to work seamlessly with Prometheus, allowing users to establish baselines and detect anomalies efficiently at scale. Users can implement this open-source solution by adding specific recording and alerting rules to their Prometheus instances.

title: Container monitoring with Grafana: Helpful resources to get started
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: Containers package software to run applications consistently across different environments, often using microservices for better performance and flexibility. Grafana helps monitor these containerized environments by collecting and visualizing metrics, which aids in troubleshooting and optimizing performance. The blog offers resources and guides for using Grafana with Docker, Kubernetes, and Helm Charts to help users get started effectively.

title: The Art of Finishing
author: Tomas Stropus
summary: The author discusses the challenge of completing projects, often getting stuck in a cycle of starting new ones instead. He shares strategies to overcome this struggle, like defining what "done" means and setting deadlines. The goal is to build habits that help him finish projects and grow as a developer.

title: Why Scrum is Stressing You Out
author: Adam Ard
summary: Scrum can increase stress for developers because it creates constant, back-to-back deadlines without breaks. This lack of autonomy and preparation time leads to a feeling of being overwhelmed and unprepared for tasks. To reduce stress, developers need to regain control over their work and processes.

title: OAuth from First Principles
author: Stack Auth
summary: OAuth is a secure way for apps to access user data without sharing passwords. It uses access tokens to grant limited permissions and ensures that the user confirms the access request. This process helps protect users from attacks like credential exposure and unauthorized access.

title: Reduce costs, optimize log volumes, and maintain full observability: Introducing Adaptive Logs
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: Grafana Labs has introduced Adaptive Logs, a new feature in Grafana Cloud that helps reduce log volumes and costs while maintaining system visibility. It uses AI to analyze log patterns and provides recommendations on which unnecessary logs can be dropped. This tool is available for all Grafana Cloud tiers, including the free tier, making it easier for users to manage their logs effectively.

title: A queryless experience for exploring metrics, logs, traces, and profiles: Introducing the Explore apps suite for Grafana
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: Grafana Labs has launched a new suite of Explore apps that makes it easier for users to access metrics, logs, traces, and profiles without complex queries. These tools allow users to quickly gain insights through simple, point-and-click interactions, simplifying the observability process. The Explore apps suite includes Explore Metrics, Explore Logs, Explore Traces, and Explore Profiles, all designed to enhance user experience and troubleshooting in Grafana.

title: Better root cause analysis: Mastering alert insights with the new central history timeline
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: Grafana has introduced a new "History" feature in version 11.2, allowing users to view the state transitions of all alert rules in one place. This feature helps with root cause analysis by showing when alerts fired or stopped, making it easier to identify issues and improve incident response. Users can filter events, zoom in on specific time periods, and access detailed information about each alert rule.

title: How to say hello
author: James Buckhouse
summary: Saying hello can greatly impact your life by shaping first impressions, which are formed quickly and can last a long time. To make a positive first impression, focus on your voice, body language, and genuine curiosity in conversations. Every greeting is an opportunity to connect, learn, and potentially build a meaningful relationship.

title: Grafana Alloy 1.3 release: Debug pipelines in real time
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: Grafana Alloy 1.3 has been released, introducing live debugging for real-time monitoring of data pipelines. This feature allows users to visualize data transformations, identify errors, and analyze pipeline behavior more efficiently. Users can enable live debugging in their configuration to streamline their development process.

title: Bootstrapping Talos Linux over SSH
author: Scott Lowe
summary: Talos Linux is a specialized Linux distribution for running Kubernetes, typically bootstrapped via the Talos API. If direct network access to the nodes isn't possible, you can use SSH tunneling as a workaround. This involves modifying machine configurations to include a specific certificate and using SSH port forwarding to bootstrap the cluster.

title: The magic of small engineering teams
author: James Temperton
summary: Small engineering teams at PostHog are small, speedy, and autonomous, allowing for fast shipping and scalability while maintaining a startup culture. Each small team has a clear mission, runs itself with minimal management layers, and prioritizes speed and ownership. Tradeoffs like overlap and fuzzy ownership are accepted to prioritize speed and innovation.

title: Fear of over-engineering has killed engineering altogether
author: fika.bar
summary: The article discusses how the fear of over-engineering has led to a lack of thoughtful engineering practices in tech. It emphasizes the importance of basic calculations, or "Napkin Math," to make informed decisions and avoid costly mistakes during development. The author argues that finding a balance between rapid shipping and proper engineering can lead to better outcomes.

title: Reverse Engineering For Everyone!
author: 0xinfection.github.io
summary: Reverse engineering is the process of analyzing an object to understand its design and function. This tutorial set aims to simplify the learning of reverse engineering for beginners and those wanting to refresh their skills. It covers various architectures and is available for download in PDF or MOBI formats.

title: Monitor these Kubernetes signals to help rightsize your fleet
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary: Organizations using Kubernetes should monitor resource usage to optimize costs and reduce environmental impact. Key signs of under- or over-provisioning include CPU usage, network latency, and idle resources. Regular monitoring and adjustment are essential for maintaining an efficient and sustainable Kubernetes environment.

title: My Recommended Kubernetes Resources for Newbies
author: Marcus Noble
summary: Marcus Noble shares his recommended resources for learning Kubernetes, aimed at beginners. He suggests various books, tutorials, video channels, and conferences to help newcomers get started. Noble encourages readers to share their own favorite resources as well.

title: Book: Just Enough Software Architecture
author: George Fairbanks
summary: This book on software architecture emphasizes risk-driven architecting and democratizes architecture to make it relevant to all developers. It cultivates declarative knowledge and focuses on the technical aspects of software development to help builders make principled design tradeoffs. The book provides practical advice on building models and analyzing architectures to ensure system success.

title: Design Docs at Google
author: Malte Ubl
summary: Unstructured text in the form of design docs can help solve problems early in a project by providing concise and easy-to-understand communication of problems and solutions at a higher level than code. Design docs at Google serve various functions like identifying design issues early, achieving consensus, scaling knowledge, and forming an organizational memory around design decisions. It's essential for design docs to be detailed enough but also short to ensure they are read and not mistaken for implementation manuals.

title: How to customize your Loki deployment with Ansible
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary:
Michal Vaško is a DevOps engineer at cloudWerkstatt, with a passion for open source technology and a deep love for observability.
While operations or platform teams have long relied on visibility into metrics to react swiftly, the idea of doing the same thing with logs was once just a dream. Thankfully, Grafana Loki has revolutionized the logging stack, giving you the same level of visibility with logs that you get with metrics.
If you haven’t embarked on the Loki journey yet, now is the time with the release of Loki 3.0!
There are several deployment methods available for various deployment modes: Helm, Tanka, Docker or Docker Compose, local, and from source. For more details on all these methods, you can refer to the Grafana Loki installation guide.
All these installation methods are great, serving their purpose and providing flexibility to users so you can deploy Loki in a manner that fits your specific scenario. But let me introduce you to another approach — the Ansible Loki Role. This role supports Debian, U...

title: Endpoint Selectors and Kubernetes Namespaces in CiliumNetworkPolicies
author: Scott Lowe
summary: The behavior of endpoint selectors in CiliumNetworkPolicies can be influenced by Kubernetes namespaces. An empty endpoint selector in a policy selects endpoints only within the same namespace. To target endpoints in another namespace, you must explicitly specify the source endpoint's namespace in the policy.

title: Queueing
author: Encore Updates
summary: An interactive study of queueing strategies

title: Ben Franklin: The Thirteen Necessary Virtues
author: Farnam Street
summary: In "The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin," Franklin outlines thirteen virtues he deemed necessary or desirable, including temperance, silence, order, resolution, frugality, industry, sincerity, justice, moderation, cleanliness, tranquillity, chastity, and humility. He suggested focusing on one virtue at a time to master them sequentially, with temperance being the starting point. Franklin believed acquiring these virtues would lead to self-improvement and the ability to navigate life's challenges with wisdom and integrity.

title: How to explore metrics without PromQL queries in Grafana
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary:
At GrafanaCON 2024, Grafana founder Torkel Ödegaard introduced Grafana 11, which has a feature set that aligns with the same goals we’ve had since the OSS project launched in 2013. 
“The core mission of Grafana that we’ve had from the start is to make observability easy and powerful through good UX design, a focus on ease of use, and user flexibility and freedom,” Torkel said. 
Throughout the years we’ve approached this in various ways over the years — by creating powerful query editors that are easier to use; improving ways to build panels and dashboards; updating how you navigate data; or making it easier to explore or connect dashboards together by data links.
But we always ask how can Grafana do better? It can take some time to learn how to build dashboards, and even the most advanced dashboards can sometimes be a little too static. So what if Grafana could do it all for you dynamically and on the fly?


In Grafana 11, the latest major release which is now generally available, we’re excited to introduce Expl...

title: Grafana Alerting: new tools to resolve incidents faster and avoid alert fatigue
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary:
The maturity of your alerting strategy has a direct impact on the reliability of your infrastructure and your applications. It can also have a big impact on engineering productivity. So whether you’re talking about resolving incidents faster or avoiding alerting fatigue, alerting should always be front and center.
With Grafana Alerting, you can alert on logs and metrics no matter where your data is stored, which makes it a powerful tool for consolidating and automating how you observe your system. In recent months we’ve worked hard to make it easier to create, manage, and triage alerts. We’ve also looked to address the needs of enterprise users that want scalability around as-code deployments and support for multiple teams working in the same environment.
In this blog post, we’ll recap some of the exciting updates we’ve made on the road to Grafana 11, which is now generally available. These upgrades can help you identify and resolve issues faster, and improve the quality of life for the engineers who get notifie...

title: If Inheritance is so bad, why does everyone use it?
author: buttondown.email
summary: The essay discusses the drawbacks of inheritance and suggests banning it entirely, highlighting problems with conventional class-based inheritance. It explores the historical origins of inheritance in OOP languages like SIMULA-67 and Eiffel, pointing out potential improvements in inheritance implementation. The text also touches on the evolution of inheritance-related concepts like abstract data types and modules, emphasizing the need for better language design.

title: Learning about distributed systems: where to start?
author: Visit profile
summary: The text emphasizes a principled approach to learning distributed systems over a quick, code-focused method. It suggests starting with foundational concepts like predicate logic and impossibility results before delving into algorithms like Paxos and studying time and state management. The author recommends moving on to cloud computing frameworks and databases after building a strong understanding of distributed systems fundamentals.

title: Why you need a "WTF Notebook"
author: Simpler Machines
summary: The "WTF Notebook" technique involves keeping a journal where you note down things that seem odd or problematic in a new team without immediately addressing them. By observing, listening, and compiling a list of issues, you gain insights and avoid being perceived as overly critical. The process involves identifying simple solutions, discussing unresolved issues with the team, and gradually addressing more complex problems with empathy and collaboration. This method helps in establishing credibility, building a reputation as a problem solver, and effectively making positive changes within a team.

title: Find your logs data with Explore Logs: No LogQL required!
author: Grafana Labs Blog on Grafana Labs
summary:
We are thrilled to announce the preview of Explore Logs, a new way to browse your logs without writing LogQL. In this post, we’ll cover why we built Explore Logs and we’ll dive deeper into some of its features, including at-a-glance breakdowns by label, detected fields, and our new pattern detection. At the end, we’ll tell you how you can try Explore Logs for yourself today.
But let’s start from the beginning — with good old LogQL.
We love LogQL
Grafana Loki, Grafana Labs’ open source log aggregation project, provides a powerful query language called LogQL. Site reliability engineers (SREs) and other Loki experts love to use it to filter logs for specific keywords, reduce noise by selecting specific labels, and perform other operations to get answers to understand their systems.
Metrics can be created from logs, which are put into dashboards to visualize key insights. Alerts can be set up and wired into Grafana Incident Response & Management (IRM), which includes Grafana OnCall and Grafana Incident, so you can m...

title: 8 Top Docker Tips & Tricks for 2024
author: Jason Dunne
summary: In this article, the author shares their top 8 tips and tricks for using Docker in 2024. They discuss various ways to optimize Docker, such as using Docker Desktop for Mac 4.6 to improve file sharing speed, strategically layering instructions in Dockerfiles to optimize caching, and avoiding unnecessary files in the build context to reduce build times. The author also highlights the benefits of using Docker Init to streamline project setups, Docker Scout for proactive vulnerability detection, Docker Build Cloud for faster and consistent builds, and Docker Debug for troubleshooting and debugging. These tips and tricks aim to enhance productivity, efficiency, and security in Docker usage.

title: Planning fallacy
author: wikipedia.org
summary: The text discusses the planning fallacy, which is a phenomenon where individuals tend to be overly optimistic and underestimate the time needed to complete future tasks. This bias is seen in both personal and group projects, and it involves underestimating time, costs, and risks while overestimating benefits. Various studies and explanations are presented, including how people focus on optimistic scenarios, engage in wishful thinking, and have memory biases that lead to underestimation. Strategies such as forming implementation intentions have been found to reduce the planning fallacy by encouraging earlier task initiation and reducing interruptions.

title: In defense of simple architectures
author: danluu.com
summary: Wave, a $1.7B company with 70 engineers, emphasizes a simple architecture focusing on a Python monolith on top of Postgres to handle its CRUD app. Despite the trend towards complex architectures, Wave's success showcases the efficiency and scalability of simple systems, even at high-traffic levels. The company's deliberate choices on tools like Python, RabbitMQ, and Kubernetes highlight their commitment to managing complexity where it adds value, such as in telecom integrations, while maintaining straightforward solutions in other areas like API design with GraphQL. Their experience underscores the benefits of simplicity in architecture, allowing resources to be allocated where complexity truly benefits the business.

title: If Architects had to work like Programmers
author: Gunnar Anzinger
summary: The document is a humorous letter that imagines what it would be like if architects had to work like programmers. The letter is written from the perspective of a client who wants a house designed and built, but is unclear about the specifics and wants the architect to use their discretion. The letter includes a number of contradictory requests and vague instructions, and ends with the client suggesting that they may actually want a travel trailer instead of a house.

title: How is a binary executable organized? Let's explore it!
author: Julia Evans
summary: Executable file formats are regular file formats that can be understood with the right tools. This article explores the organization of binary executables, using ELF binaries on Linux as an example. It explains symbols, sections, and segments, and how to use tools like readelf and objdump to investigate them. It also covers some basic assembly code and how programs are organized into segments.

title: The Shirky Principle: Institutions Try to Preserve the Problem to Which They Are the Solution
author: effectiviology.com
summary: The Shirky Principle is the observation that "institutions will try to preserve the problem to which they are the solution," meaning that entities tend to prolong the problem they are solving. This can lead to unintended consequences, such as government agencies hindering attempts by others to address an issue to ensure their relevance or a company resisting attempts to automate a process to ensure an employee remains necessary. The principle has implications in various domains, including business and politics, and understanding it can help predict and modify behavior.

title: My productivity app is a never-ending .txt file
author: Jeff Huang
summary: The author explains their productivity system, which revolves around a text file that serves as a to-do list, research notebook, and meeting minutes all in one. They use an online calendar to keep track of future plans and schedule, and every night, they create a daily to-do list by taking all the items on their calendar for the next day and appending it to the text file. The daily list also doubles as a record of everything they have ever done, and they use various shorthands and tags to make it easily searchable. They also discuss their email workflow and how they handle incoming messages.

title: Mental Models: The Best Way to Make Intelligent Decisions (~100 Models Explained)
author: Farnam Street
summary: Mental models are simplified representations of how things work that help us make intelligent decisions. These models distill complex ideas into manageable concepts and aid in understanding the world around us. By applying various mental models, such as the Circle of Competence, Second-Order Thinking, and Probabilistic Thinking, individuals can enhance their decision-making processes and achieve better outcomes. Understanding and utilizing mental models from different disciplines, such as physics, biology, systems thinking, numeracy, microeconomics, and human nature, can provide valuable insights and improve our ability to navigate complex scenarios effectively.

title: Is Obsidian the True Second Brain? ft. Nick Milo
author: Tiago Forte
summary: The article discusses how obsidian, a second brain app, can be used to help organize and develop creative projects, specifically a TV show. The author and Nick Milo, an obsidian expert, discuss how obsidian allows for organizing notes through relationships rather than just time, and demonstrate how to use obsidian to create a map or hub of notes related to the TV show project. They also discuss the importance of clustering related notes and creating headers to establish relationships between them.

title: I'm an Old Fart and AI Makes Me Sad
author: alex_suzuki
summary: The author longs for the simpler days of technology like PCs and the early Internet, but feels overwhelmed and excluded by the complex nature of AI. They are concerned about becoming dependent on AI products that they cannot fully understand or control.

title: How to hire low experience, high potential people
author: Tara Seshan
summary: When hiring low experience, high potential individuals, it is important to look for specific qualities and assess their potential. One key factor is finding candidates who have made a significant impact in their previous roles and can separate their actions from the overall team's performance. Additionally, it is beneficial to hire people who have taken unconventional paths and can explain their choices coherently. Look for individuals with a chip on their shoulder, who have something to prove and possess a sense of security. High emotional intelligence and persuasion skills are also valuable traits to consider. Lastly, seek candidates who have demonstrated excellence in any area, as this shows their drive and self-discipline. It is crucial to assess their openness to feedback and their ability to not take themselves too seriously.

title: (Almost) Every infrastructure decision I endorse or regret after 4 years running infrastructure at a startup
author: Jack Lindamood
summary: The author of this document shares their experiences and insights regarding infrastructure decisions made during their four years of leading infrastructure at a startup. They discuss various decisions, such as choosing AWS over Google Cloud, endorsing the use of EKS for Kubernetes clusters, regretting the use of EKS managed addons, endorsing the use of RDS and Redis ElastiCache for data management, endorsing the use of AWS VPN for simplicity, regretting the high cost of AWS premium support, endorsing the use of Control Tower Account Factory for Terraform, endorsing the practice of monthly cost tracking meetings, regretting the use of Datadog for its expense, endorsing the use of Ubuntu for dev servers, endorsing the use of AppSmith for automating processes, endorsing the use of Helm for packaging and deploying Kubernetes objects, endorsing the use of OCI stored Helm charts, regretting not using OpenTelemetry early on, endorsing the use of Renovatebot for dependency updates, endorsing the use of Kubernetes for ho...

title: Building Your Second Brain with Obsidian: A Guide Inspired by Tiago Forte
author: Milind Gunjan
summary: In this guide inspired by Tiago Forte's book "Building a Second Brain," the note-taking app Obsidian is recommended to create a powerful second brain for managing knowledge effectively. The guide provides step-by-step instructions for using Obsidian, including organizing notes with folders and categories, implementing the PARA framework, using bi-directional links, enhancing organization with tags, and mastering progressive summarization. The guide also recommends developing a Zettelkasten system and making time for review and refinement. By following this guide, users can build a powerful second brain in Obsidian to improve productivity and generate new insights.

title: Reading QR codes without a computer!
author: blinry.org
summary: This document provides an interactive explanation of how to read QR codes without a computer. It covers topics such as the anatomy of a QR code, mask patterns, encoding modes, reading order, decoding the length, and decoding the content. It also includes a step-by-step guide with examples and a cheat sheet. The document concludes by congratulating the reader on learning how to decode QR codes by hand and providing options to practice or scan QR codes.

title: Say Goodbye to Docker Volumes 👋
author: DEV Community
summary: Docker has released a new feature called Docker Compose Watch, which allows for automatic synchronization of local source code with code in a Docker container without the need for volumes. This feature introduces a new attribute called watch, which contains rules for watching paths and executing actions when files change. The actions include synchronization, rebuilding, and synchronization followed by restarting the container. However, the watch attribute currently does not support glob patterns. To further improve Docker setups, collaboration can be promoted through the use of Docker extensions like Livecycle. It is also important to follow best practices with Dockerfiles and utilize a .dockerignore file.

title: You probably had used DoTheSimplestThingThatCouldPossiblyWorkFirst.
author: c2.com
summary: - (if you're not sure what to do yet) Beware: The history and therefore meaning of this phrase is lost on many people who wield it. The 'if you're not sure what to do yet' part tends to be forgotten.

title: 28 Mental Models That Changed My Life
author: Alex Brogan

title: Ask yourself dumb questions –…
author: What's new
summary: When learning mathematics, the focus is often on the polished end product, but the process of discovery is messy and involves pursuing naive or fruitless directions. It is important to not ignore these "failed" lines of inquiry, as they contribute to a deeper understanding of the topic. Asking "stupid" questions challenges conventional wisdom and can lead to surprising conclusions or a better understanding of why the conventional wisdom exists. When listening to a seminar, asking "dumb" but constructive questions can help clarify issues and show engagement. However, questions that do not enhance the flow of the talk are best saved for after the presentation.

title: Marcus Aurelius: The Man Who Solved the Universe
author: Horses
summary: Marcus Aurelius, a Roman Emperor and philosopher, was known for his contributions to stoicism and his book "Meditations." Despite being in a position of power, Aurelius chose to live a life of virtue and resisted indulging in hedonistic pursuits. He believed in living in accordance with nature and fulfilling one's potential. Aurelius emphasized the importance of kindness, understanding, and resilience in the face of adversity. He also cautioned against placing too much value on material possessions and encouraged reflection on the inevitability of death. Stoicism, as a philosophy, focused on finding happiness through inner virtue rather than external factors.

title: The Usefulness of Useless Knowledge
author: Abraham Flexner
summary: In "The Usefulness of Useless Knowledge," Abraham Flexner questions why people continue to pursue intellectual and creative endeavors despite the presence of destructive forces in the world. He argues that intellectual and spiritual pursuits, which may seem useless on the surface, often lead to unexpected utility. Flexner provides examples of scientists, mathematicians, and artists who were driven by curiosity rather than practical applications, yet their work ultimately resulted in significant advancements. He emphasizes the importance of cultivating curiosity and the pursuit of knowledge for its own sake, rather than solely focusing on immediate practical applications.

title: 100 tiny changes to transform your life: from the one-minute rule to pyjama yoga
author: Guardian Staff
summary: The article provides 100 small changes that can transform one's life. These changes range from not setting a morning alarm to incorporating mobility snacks into one's day, and from listening to classical music to walking outdoors every day. The changes aim to improve mental and physical health, productivity, creativity, and overall well-being. The article highlights that small, intentional changes can have a significant impact on one's life.

title: On Tyranny
author: Timothy Snyder
summary: "On Tyranny" is a collection of twenty lessons from the twentieth century that were written to provide guidance on defending democracy and the rule of law. The lessons cover a range of topics, including not obeying in advance, defending institutions, supporting the multiple-party system, being vigilant of paramilitaries, and believing in truth. The author emphasizes the importance of taking responsibility, being reflective, and staying informed. The book has been updated to address recent events and is available in a graphic edition.

title: Here Are My Favorite Books, Movies, and Music of 2023
author: Barack Obama
summary: The content includes a list of favorite books, movies, and music of 2023. The list includes notable books such as "The Heaven and Earth Grocery Store" by James McBride and "Poverty, By America" by Matthew Desmond, movies like "Rustin" and "Leave the World Behind," and songs like "TQG" by Karol G & Shakira and "I Remember Everything" by Zach Bryan ft. Kacey Musgraves.

title: Thirty Things I’ve Learned
author: Nick Crocker
summary: In this article, the author shares thirty lessons they have learned throughout their life. Some of the key takeaways include the importance of gratitude, regular exercise, and writing down one's thoughts for clarity. The author also emphasizes the significance of surrounding oneself with the right people, asking for what you want, and not being disheartened in the face of challenges. They discuss the value of time, self-control, and listening, as well as the impact of controlling one's inputs and being genuinely curious. The author concludes by highlighting the importance of paying attention to one's actions when alone, getting outside, and the value of making something.

title: 100 Little Ideas
author: Morgan Housel
summary: The content is a list of various ideas from different fields that help explain how the world works, including the Depressive Realism, the Curse of Knowledge, the Pareto Principle, the Golem Effect, the Dunning-Kruger Effect, and more. These ideas offer insights into human behavior, decision-making, and biases.

title: Five Things I Learned in 2023
author: David Chen
summary: In this reflection on the year 2023, the author shares five things they have learned. First, they discuss the fragility of industries like Hollywood and the media industry, which have been disrupted and are on the verge of collapse. Second, they highlight how bad people seem to own everything and use their power to make the world worse. Third, they point out the temptation to think that those in charge know what they're doing, even when they make catastrophic decisions. Fourth, they discuss the lack of thought and oversight in the implementation of AI, leading to misinformation and potential harm. title: Power of Tokens:Refresh Tokens and Access Tokens in Backend Development
author: Nilesh Raut
summary: Refresh Tokens and Access Tokens are two important concepts in backend development. Access Tokens grant immediate access to specific resources or functionalities, while Refresh Tokens can be exchanged for a new access token. When a user logs in, they receive both an access token and a refresh token. The access token has a short lifespan for enhanced security, while the refresh token has an extended validity as a safety net. In practice, the refresh token allows for seamless user experience by automatically obtaining a fresh access token when the previous one expires. Understanding these tokens is crucial for building robust and secure applications.

title: How to get creative (without doing drugs):
author: George Mack
summary: Getting creative doesn't require drugs, but rather a shift in mindset and approach. Instead of treating creativity like productivity, where we work harder and expect ideas to appear, we should focus on adding new inputs. This can be done through techniques like the Swedish House Mafia Technique, where ideas are bounced back and forth in a collaborative setting, or Balaji's Transformer, where ideas are transformed from one form to another (e.g. writing to drawing). Other strategies include creating an evil twin to explore new ideas, waking up early or staying up late for peak creativity, studying history for a broader range of inputs, avoiding toxic and dramatic people, consuming niche content, spinning wheels with thought-provoking questions, and not identifying too closely with ideas.

title: Risk Management is not Project Management
author: Rucker's Musings
summary: Risk management and project management are often confused, leading to the misallocation of accountability in project planning. While it is common to involve third parties in project delivery, the ultimate responsibility for project success lies with the client or project owner. Shifting all accountability to a third party may seem appealing, but it does not eliminate the client's responsibility and can actually increase the risk of project failure. Successful project management involves clear communication of risks and shared responsibility among all parties involved.

title: More product, fewer product managers
author: ycombinator.com
summary: Product managers often fail to bridge the gap between engineering and the user because they focus too much on administrative tasks rather than hands-on work. A good product manager should actively engage with users, gather continuous feedback, and plan and execute product launches. They should also effectively communicate user feedback to engineering, understanding the project's current status, future direction, and necessary changes. However, many product managers rely on documentation and administrative tasks, resembling project managers rather than true product managers.

title: More product, fewer PMs
author: Kitemaker
summary: The discussion around the number of Product Managers (PMs) required in a product team has gained momentum, with examples like Airbnb restructuring their product management organization and startups thriving without any PMs. It is argued that many companies hire too many PMs, resulting in them being bogged down with project management tasks rather than optimizing the product. The ideal time to hire a PM at a startup is when the founders can no longer be involved in all important product decisions. This approach also requires a shift in responsibility for the product, with design and engineering teams actively participating in shaping the product. Practices such as starting together, exposing everyone to users, and managing the team effectively can help create more product-oriented teams. It is important to avoid overestimating the number of PMs needed, as too many can steal the product focus away from designers and engineers.

However, they highlight the problem of relying on chains of assumptions to determine what actions will be impactful. The author emphasizes the importance of thinking from first principles and questioning assumptions to build a stronger chain of assumptions.

title: Helm is flawed and here is why
author: Jacco Taal
summary: Helm's design is flawed because it treats YAML files as simple text files and does not take into account the structure and meaning of the YAML. The template engine used by Helm does not recognize that the files are YAML and requires additional instructions, such as nindent, to maintain the correct indentation. Additionally, Helm's template language lacks knowledge of Kubernetes resources and YAML, resulting in unreadable and error-prone template files. This flawed design could have been avoided if Helm had evolved into a tool that allowed Kubernetes resources to be written as code in a modern programming language, providing benefits such as functions and abstraction.

title: Quoting Ted Sanders
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered:
Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra
[...] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7.
— Ted Sanders, explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions

title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
GitHub Octoverse 2026
I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave  me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular:

This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month.
The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: 

Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location. Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...]
Industry. Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...]
Interoperability. Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation.

title: Getting good at AI takes time and practice
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Many people think1 that getting “good at AI” is trivial. Sure, with some early models there were tricks you had to learn,2 but current models don’t need them. Even if there are different tricks3 that work on current models, the next generation will render them obsolete, so why bother? Just tell the model what you want it to do.
This take is particularly popular with the anti-AI crowd, who scoff4 at the idea that AI-reluctant people are being left behind, or that it might be irresponsible to advise other engineers to avoid AI use entirely. According to them, if AI does ever become capable enough to be worth using, they’ll be able to start using it with no learning curve. Is that right?
No. Like most things, getting good at using AI isn’t just about clever tricks. It requires developing long-term skills5, which takes time and practice.
Supplying the right context
One failure mode I’ve seen with people who are new to AI is expecting it to read their mind: for instance, asking it to “solve my issue” without ever saying what the issue is, or asking it about some Slack-related problem without actually connecting your agent to Slack. Agents are flexible and will try their absolute hardest to guess what problem you’re facing and how to solve it, but the guesses will be largely wrong. Skilled AI users will pick up on the fact that the agent is missing key context and backtrack.
Skilled AI users will also reflexively include why they want to achieve their current goal, so that the agent has enough context to make decisions. This is often non-trivial: most of us know what we want to do but have to take a second to think about the broader reasons behind it.
Knowing what the model can and can’t do

title: Laypeople support technical fields for technology, not art
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Some people think that LLMs should not be used in technical fields like programming or mathematics, because those fields are actually art. True or not, this kind of argument is not going to be persuasive to the general population. The argument goes something1 like this:

It doesn’t matter how effective LLMs are at technical fields like programming or mathematics, because one of the essential values of those fields is that they’re art. While it looks to laypeople like these fields exist to solve practical problems, what they’re actually for is to produce works of beauty, or to express something distinctively human, or to spend time contemplating the infinite. Simply solving the problems misses the point in the same way that building an infinite poem generator would miss the point of poetry.

I agree that programming or mathematics can be beautiful. I remember being mildly awestruck at learning epsilon-delta proofs, and I have written a lot about the kind of software I think is elegant. Since there’s no clear definition of art or of aesthetics in general, it’s plausible to me that almost everything could have an artistic dimension to it.
All of this is compelling to software engineers, many of whom (like me) find some programs beautiful and are flattered to think of themselves as artists. But I suspect it’s spectacularly uncompelling to onlookers, because it undermines the implicit reasons that they have for supporting technical fields. Many people who are not programmers or mathematicians think of those fields like this:

I enjoy the fruits of technology: modern medicine, transport, mobile phones, and so on
While I don’t understand the exact relationship, I know that technical fields like mathematics and programming are essential to sustaining and advancing these technologies
Therefore I’m happy to respect and support mathematicians in their mysterious research work
And I’m broadly okay with2 software engineers drawing healthy salaries for the same reason

title: My obituary for programming
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
My obituary for programming
Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code:

Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible.

If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving.
If those many problems were a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real.

title: AI is driving a boom in modestly successful software projects
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
If AI is so great, why aren’t we seeing an explosion of new, amazing software products? If anyone can turn their idea into working software with coding agents, where is all that software? People have been asking this question for years. As far as I can tell, the answer is that it’s spread out over a lot of modestly successful projects:

Somewhere between 2x and 20x new software is being created, depending on where you look
There’s no real growth in massively successful software projects (not counting AI tools)
There is around 2x growth in modestly successful software projects

Where all the new software is
I picked1 around twenty separate sources — software marketplaces, plugin registries, modding platforms, etc — which expose installation counts. I then compared the number2 of successful software projects between 2022-24 and 2025-26: i.e. before and after agentic coding hit the mainstream in mid-2025.
There’s a clear jump in modestly (not wildly) successful projects. For instance, the NVDA screen-reader addons directory had a bit over twice as many new addons with more than a thousand downloads (though no change in addons with more than ten thousand). The HACS open-source home automation community plugins store likewise saw twice as many new addons with over a hundred installs but no change in ones with over a thousand. New Steam games with over a hundred reviews are about 60% more common now than pre-2024. Obsidian plugins, Firefox and Chrome extensions, Nexus game mods, and Blender extensions had the same pattern. The Google Play store, WordPress plugins, and a few others didn’t show this pattern, but I think it’s still enough to conclude that AI is indeed driving a boom in hobbyist software.
Why addons and plugins?
I think examining addons, mods, and plugins is useful for a few reasons. First, it’s usually pretty easy to tell how many people are using them, or at least have installed them. Obviously AI is letting people produce a lot of software — I work at G...

author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly).
I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development:

Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...]
This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before.  [...[
With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks.

title: i love writing
author: lauren
summary:
i love writing. i never let agents write for me. whether it's docs, or tweets, or shitposts, or even prompts (okay maybe that one's harder as agents manage other agents) 

there's a simple reason for that: i still strongly believe that writing is thinking. it's a skill i hope to never give up. it's also important to me that whatever i say is always authentic, mistakes and all. my favorite posts are the ones that i just full send without any editing

i suspect it also helps with prompting. being able to clearly express what i want, and knowing the vocabulary i need to be able to direct my agents does seem to make for more effective usage of agents. in the same way that engineers have an advantage when we prompt agents to write code, because we are intimately familiar with the words that make up the discipline

knowing the right word incantations to get an agent to produce a desired goal almost feels like spellcasting. as models get more capable, and that input box looks more and more like a magic box that can output anything, words become the interface between you and the genie

there may come a time when we give up the keyboard in exchange for brain-computer interfaces. but until then, i'm writing every word.

title: I am a member of the Norwegian Nobel Committee
author: Peter Girnus 🦅
summary:
I am a member of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

There are five of us. Five people, appointed by a parliament most of the planet could not find on a map, who decide, once a year, which human being the world has agreed to call good.

I know. I know. I think about it on the tram.

We meet in a building on Henrik Ibsens gate, a street named after a man who wrote almost exclusively about people discovering they are frauds, which nobody on the committee finds funny except me. There is a room with a long table and the portraits of the dead laureates looking down, Mandela, the Dalai Lama, a great many earnest men in spectacles, and one portrait we do not discuss, which is Kissinger, 1973, awarded while the bombs were still falling, after which two of our predecessors resigned and the satirist Tom Lehrer said political satire was now obsolete. We keep him on the wall. A reminder. Every family has the uncle.

It is October in Oslo, which means the sun gives up around four in the afternoon like a civil servant, and it rains the particular Norwegian rain that isn’t quite falling, just hanging there, judging you. I arrive with wet shoes. I always arrive with wet shoes. There is coffee, because this is Norway and there is always coffee, we drink more of it per person than almost anyone alive, and someone’s wife has sent kanelboller, the cinnamon buns, and we sit, five Norwegians, damp, caffeinated, sugared, and we decide the moral standing of the entire species.

Let me tell you how it actually works, because the world imagines a cathedral and it is, I promise you, a book club with a mandate.

287 nominations this year. 208 people, 79 organizations. title: Software engineers don't get to be Luddites about AI
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Many software engineers are righteously angry about AI. It’s understandable to be upset that the skills you built your professional identity around are getting automated away. But software engineers are the last people in the world who should be complaining about this. If you live by the sword, you will perish by the sword1.
Software engineering has always automated industries
From the very beginning, software engineering has been about automating other people’s work. Every single commercial software program2 is valuable because it takes over some task you would have to pay a human to do. The engineer who built VisiCalc, one of the first pieces of personal commercial software, agonized over the potential of the spreadsheet to put bookkeepers out of work. Here is a brief list of industries software engineers have automated away3:

Video rental stores
Business directories and encyclopaedias
Typesetting companies
Travel agencies
Record stores
Typing pools
Data-entry
Trading-floor runners

Now that it’s our turn, should we bluster and complain that software engineering is a priceless art that should not be automated? Come off it. No crying in the casino.
The Luddites and the mechanics
Many software engineers have adopted the cause of the Luddites. I’ve written about the Luddites a few times, but in short: they were a group of professional textile workers who found themselves displaced by the advent of textile automation like power looms, knitting frames, and shearing machines. To software engineers worried about being displaced by automation, the Luddites seem like heroes4. But software engineers aren’t like the textile workers in this scenario! We are like the smiths and mechanics who built the power looms in the first place.
Ironically, those mechanics were themselves automated away fifty years after the Luddite uprising, in almost an exact parallel. Improvements to the manufacturing process meant that unskilled boys and labourers — so-called “illegal men” —  could...

title: War Through Weakness

title: Don't diagnose your opponents
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
When you disagree with someone, there are two paths forward. The first is to try to engage with what they’re saying: what their reasons are, whether their position is true, what evidence could be brought to bear, and so on. The second is to diagnose them: to engage with the second-order question of why they’re saying it. For instance, if you’re arguing with somebody about microservices1, you could say “well, you only like microservices because you want to polish your resume”, or “you only like monoliths because you’re scared of distributed systems”.
This happens a lot in online arguments. On the question “are AI models improving”, some anti-AI people will argue that people only think so because AI psychosis is rotting their brain, and the dumber they get, the smarter AI models seem in comparison. Likewise, many pro-AI people argue that people only disagree because they’re Luddites, or scared of change, and so on. None of these arguments are about the quality of AI models.
It feels so good to diagnose your opponents because there’s no possible response. If you say “I think AI models are improving because these benchmark scores are rising”, somebody might point out that the AI labs are training on those benchmarks, or argue that they represent isolated skills that don’t transfer, and so on, making you feel stupid. If you say “you only disagree with me because you want to roleplay as a revolutionary”, how could you be proven wrong? The more someone protests a diagnosis, the more it sounds like it must be right. Otherwise why would they be so upset?
Of course, they’re so upset precisely because there is no possible response. By moving to diagnosis, you’re no longer having an argument about the facts, you’re purely in the area of rhetoric. But when you’re in the middle of an argument, diagnosing always feels like you’re being piercingly analytical. It feels like you’re cutting right to the heart of the matter: these complicated arguments are just chaff, intended to di...

title: We're going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
Here's a product feature which the world is going to need a whole lot more of over the coming months and years: default hard budget caps. I'm talking about the feature of pay-by-usage services and APIs that lets you say "after $X/month, cut this thing off and return errors". These need to be hard limits. Soft caps, "after $X/month, send me a warning email", will not cut it.
Coding agents, and personal agents (coding agents wrapped in a less threatening UI), greatly reduce the friction of spinning up code that can do useful things. Sometimes those things cost money - calls to paid APIs, or hosted web applications, or systems that can bill for additional storage and compute.
Nobody wants to wake up to an email sent at midnight warning about a budget limit and find that, while they slept, their rogue service had consumed several hundred (or several thousand) more dollars of usage.
An argument against this is that businesses don't want their hosted applications to start throwing errors because some budget was exceeded. I expect that most businesses and individuals would prefer errors to a surprise $10,000+ bill.
I think hard budget caps need to be the default. If someone wants to live dangerously they should be able to do that, but it needs to be on an opt-in basis. Have a nice, clear checkbox somewhere prominent:

 Remove the budget cap. My application will not be shut down if I exceed the configured budget limit, and I will be responsible for subsequent charges.

The service I most want to see this from is AWS. I've heard plenty of stories from people who refuse to use AWS for personal projects out of (justified) fear that a runaway service might bankrupt them. I've also heard stories from people who didn't anticipate this and ended up seriously burned.

title: Shipping is the foundation
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
There are lots of skills involved in being a successful engineer at a big tech company. Running effective meetings, writing good design docs, fleshing out tickets and epics, improving team processes, tech leading small groups of engineers, and so on. But all of these rest on the foundation of being able to ship.
In Dota 2, the early game involves “laning”: competing with an enemy player to collect resources from a small area. There are many, many strategies and considerations involved in laning. But the simplest possible approach is just to run at your opponent and attack them until they’re forced to either run away or die. All the other laning strategies must solve that problem first, because it doesn’t matter how well you play if you’re forced out of the playing area. If you get that wrong, it doesn’t matter how much else you get right.
In Magic: the Gathering and Starcraft, many players adopt an “aggro” strategy of building an attacking force as early as possible before the enemy player has time to construct a defense. That constrains the entire strategy space of the game, because it doesn’t matter how clever your plan is if it loses to aggro every time. Even when there are no aggro players in the game, the aggro strategy still shapes how the game unfolds, because the players must still design their decks and play as if they might have to deal with an early attack.
In tech companies, shipping is the equivalent of these aggressive strategies. Almost everything you might do — writing a ticket or a design doc, delegating a task to another engineer, etc — should be compared to the default strategy of just sitting down and making the change yourself. That’s why it’s critical to be able to ship: so you can just do trivial things without having to pay the coordination cost.

title: Advice to a beginning software engineer
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
In general, you should be suspicious of engineers who are trying to give you advice. Even during ordinary times, this industry is so wide and changes so quickly that nobody really knows anything for sure. And we are not in ordinary times. The advent of LLMs and AI agents is the largest change to software engineering in my professional lifetime, and possibly the largest change ever. That said, here’s my advice:

Don’t trust senior engineers who are telling you to pick political fights
Don’t play games. Keep your head down and be helpful
Be conscientious and try hard to actually understand what you’re working on
Don’t panic about AI, and don’t delegate your judgement to it
Don’t avoid AI — keep thinking!
Don’t lose hope

Don’t trust ZIRP-era advice
Most experienced software engineers today have spent the bulk of their career in the ZIRP era. This was a time when investment money flooded the industry, driving up engineer bargaining power. Big tech companies spent a lot of money and effort trying to make their engineers happy and comfortable. If you were an engineer at one of those companies, you could expect to have a decent say in what kind of work you did, and even what kind of politics your company had. Unless you worked at a handful of unusual companies (e.g. Amazon) you could expect to be practically immune from layoffs, and to only be fired after many months (sometimes years) of low performance.
A lot of advice floating around is ZIRP-era advice: either it was written during that era, or it’s written by engineers whose habits of thought were formed during that era. This kind of advice typically tells you to take a stand (e.g. to unionize1), to speak up more against “unethical technologies” like AI, and to insist on being given time to practice your craft the way you want. This was great advice in 2016, but it’s not good advice in 2026.

title: You should all be asking way more questions
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
When someone is explaining something to me, I ask on average one question every thirty seconds. I’m sure this is frustrating to some people, but it’s actually a good habit and you should do it too.
Trying to understand
Most of the questions I ask are very short, and require very short answers. Typically I’m asking for confirmation: “so when you say X, you mean Y?”, or “this X is the thing you mentioned earlier when you were saying Z?“. The point of these questions is to make sure I understand.
A small misunderstanding early on balloons into a big misunderstanding later, because all the things you misinterpret based on the first misunderstanding will become misunderstandings in their own right, and so on. That’s why you can’t just wait until someone’s finished talking and ask all your questions at once1. 
I think most people don’t ask questions because they’re not really trying to understand: they’re happy to just trust that the person they’re talking to knows what’s going on. This goes double when that person is a well-respected or more senior engineer. However, once you have skin in the game, that all changes. When you’re in a position where you are the one responsible for success or failure — where you are going to have to go away after the conversation and take a bunch of concrete actions — you will find yourself wanting to ask many questions.
Build it in your head
When someone’s explaining a plan to me at work, I am usually building it in my head: visualizing the specific lines of code that would need to be written in order to implement it. I’ll sometimes handwave the details for solved problems (for instance, I might say “send emails like subsystem X of the same service that also sends emails”), but at minimum I’m planning out:

How data needs to flow between services (what kind of data, and how it will travel over the wire)
How services will communicate with each other (e.g. how will they auth?)
What data needs to be persisted, and where it’s going to live

title: Grafana Alerting: Scale alert routing without scaling complexity using multiple notification policies
author: Matt Jacobson
summary: Alert routing often starts simple. A team creates a few contact points, adds some label matchers, and builds a notification policy tree that sends each alert to the right destination.But alerting configurations rarely stay simple.As an organization grows, its notification policy tree must accommodate more teams, services, and routing requirements. Changes for one team still require editing a global configuration, making ownership less clear and independent provisioning harder. Over time, even small updates can require navigating an increasingly complex routing tree.With Grafana 13.2, multiple notification policies are now generally available in Grafana-managed alerting. author: Simon Willison's Weblog

Introducing Claude Opus 5
I've been offline kayaking with sea otters for much of today so I haven't had a chance to put Anthropic's new model Claude Opus 5 through its paces yet. The buzz is positive, and Anthropic's description of it as a "thoughtful and proactive model that comes close to the frontier intelligence of Claude Fable 5 at half the price" sounds promising. It's currently leading the Artificial Analysis leaderboard, in front of even Fable 5.
It's priced the same as Opus 4.8, and continues to offer a "fast mode" at twice the cost of the base model.
Based on this anecdote in the release post it sounds like it might be relentlessly proactive:

On one Frontier-Bench task, Opus 5 was given a drawing of a machine part and asked to write code to rebuild it as a 3D FreeCAD model. However, in this task, the model was intentionally given no way to directly viewthe drawing. Opus 5 responded by writing its own computer vision pipeline to pull the geometry from the raw pixels, then reconstructed the full machine part.

It's better at finding vulnerabilities but has deliberately not been trained on how to exploit them. Hopefully this means the US government won't shut it down!

As with its predecessor, Opus 4.8, we’ve intentionally avoided training Opus 5 on cyber tasks. The model has nevertheless improved substantially on these tasks as a result of becoming more generally capable, and it comes close to Mythos 5 at finding cybersecurity vulnerabilities. However, it remains substantially behind Mythos 5 on the exploitation of those vulnerabilities—that is, in turning vulnerabilities into material cyber threats.

Anthropic have published a prompting guide for Claude Opus 5.
The first pelican I got was missing the bicycle wheels; the second attempt was better.

title: LLMs reward expertise
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
In the 2010s, if you had technical gaps (say, you couldn’t write CSS), you had to either rely on a skilled colleague or just hope that the answer to your exact problem was out there on the internet. Today, everyone can write sort-of-okay CSS by delegating the task to an LLM. LLMs make everybody into a generalist.
Because of this, lots of people don’t think there’s any skill involved in working with LLMs. If you want the product that LLMs can deliver — PhD-level mathematics, pretty good but sometimes tasteless computer code, or awkward LinkedIn-style writing — you can simply ask for it. Since everyone is talking to the same models, “skilled prompters” are getting the same results as people touching LLMs for the first time.
This is wrong. The most important skill in prompting is expertise in the domain you’re prompting for.
A good illustration of this is Terence Tao’s conversation with ChatGPT about the recently-discovered counterexample to the Jacobian Conjecture. This is not the same ChatGPT I talk to! I couldn’t get to where Tao gets, even with unlimited tokens to burn.
There’s a lot to learn about good prompting from Tao’s conversation. Here are a few observations:

Tao’s messages are very short and to-the-point. He doesn’t respond point-by-point to the model, just to the gist
The model outputs are much more concise than when I try and talk to GPT-5.6 Sol about mathematics. By signalling expertise, Tao shunts the model into “talking-to-mathematicians” mode, not “explaining-to-amateurs” mode
Tao pushes back when the model’s responses look wrong, but he doesn’t directly contradict; instead, he says things like “this looks more complex than I was hoping for”
Tao makes several leaps and suggestions himself. He almost never takes the model’s advice about where to go next

title: Working with product managers
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
The relationship engineers have with product management is more dysfunctional than with any other part of the company. There’s no shared culture or language like there is with other engineers, and the rules of “who gets to tell who what to do” aren’t as clear-cut as they are with managers. Engineers don’t have a lot in common with legal, or design, or sales, but they also don’t need to interact much with those roles. In my experience, engineers are communicating with product managers almost every single day.
Against the “product mommy”
The worst version of the product/engineering relationship goes something like this:
Engineers are technically competent but are too autistic to be fully trusted. They need a kind-but-stern parental figure who knows how to communicate to other stakeholders in the organization (for instance, by being comfortable using the word “stakeholders”), and how to keep engineers from going off in the wrong direction.
This entire gross dynamic is neatly captured by the popular term “product mommy”1.
I really, really don’t like that term, or this entire dynamic in general. Almost none of my relationships with my product managers have been anything like this, though I have seen it at a distance.
Working well with product managers can be the difference between succeeding and failing at a company. Why is it so hard to maintain good relationships between engineering and product? What does a good relationship look like?
Why it’s so hard to build trust
Product managers and engineers have largely non-overlapping skillsets. Product managers don’t understand the technical work engineers do and aren’t equipped to talk about it: if an engineer gives a technical reason for something, product managers generally have to shrug and say “sure, I guess”. Likewise, engineers don’t have anything like the visibility into the organization that product managers do. Particularly in large organizations, it is the product manager who is the source of truth about who want...

title: Doing nothing at work
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
Many engineers should be doing less work. I don’t necessarily mean producing less code or fewer changes, but literally working fewer hours in the day. When they do work, they should be working at a slower pace. I like to aim to be running at 80% utilization by default: unless I have a high-pressure project going on, I spend 20% of my workday away from the computer.
High-impact opportunities
Why? Performance at tech companies is dominated by outlier events. When I think about the most impactful changes I’ve made, many of them involved a surprisingly trivial amount of work. There are no points for effort in software development. What matters is solving the right problem at the right time.
In large engineering organizations, there are usually trivial pieces of engineering work you could do that would make tens or hundreds of millions of dollars for the company. Here are three common examples:
First, when the company is trying to sign a big enterprise deal, stepping in with a feature or bugfix can make the deal happen. It doesn’t even have to be a good feature: sometimes just showing that you’re willing and able to make a concrete change will be enough.
Second, preventing or mitigating an incident early (even by just knowing the right feature flag to turn off) can save huge amounts of money: both immediate lost revenue during the incident and future lost revenue from customers who would have pulled their business or refused to sign pending contracts.

title: AI enthusiasts are in a race against time, AI skeptics are in a race against entropy
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
AI enthusiasts are in a race against time, AI skeptics are in a race against entropy
Charity Majors neatly captures the dynamic between AI enthusiasts and AI skeptics, both of whom are trying to build great software, often in the same teams:

The enthusiasts are not wrong. We are starting to see real, non-imaginary, discontinuous leaps in capabilities from teams that lean in hard to working with AI. And this does not feel like a normal technology cycle where you can wait for the dust to settle; teams that sit this out while competitors are hustling could be out of business before the dust settles. That’s a real, existential threat.
The skeptics are also not wrong. When you ship code faster than engineers can read it, in domains where nobody has full context, you are making withdrawals from a trust account that took years to build. Reliability degrades, institutional knowledge evaporates. You end up with systems nobody understands, products burbling into incoherence, and on-call rotations that grind people up and spit them out. That is ALSO a real existential threat.

Charity recommends treating this as both a leadership challenge and an engineering challenge. The key issue:

There is no natural feedback loop connecting enthusiasts with skeptics.

Designing feedback loops for an organization is a fascinating organizational design problem.
