title: Hiding Capabilities in AI Models
author: Bruce Schneier
summary:
Interesting research: “AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities”
Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. title: GPT-6.1 Terra
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
GPT-6.1 Terra
It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement.
In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use:

We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.

Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it.
Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks.
OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News:

In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select.

It often sits several layers down in a dependency tree, pulled in by a web framework, a thumbnailing service or an ML toolkit that nobody chose it for directly. On October 16, 2026, the Pillow project released version 13.0.0, and one of its security fixes is CVE-2026-112900: an argument injection in the way Pillow calls Ghostscript to render EPS images. The CVE record, published on October 19, rates it 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. It affects every Pillow release from 2.6.0 up to, but not including, 13.0.0. No exploitation in the wild has been reported so far, but CISA's assessment marks it as automatable with total technical impact.Upgrade Pillow to 13.0.0 on every project and image that handles untrusted images, and remove Ghostscript from images that do not need EPS support.This guide is for security and platform teams with Python projects on GitLab. It covers the fixed version for each distribution, how the flaw works, the other High and Critical issues fixed in the same release, how to locate affected projects with dependency scanning, container scanning, GitLab Orbit, and code search, and how to remediate at scale with GitLab Duo Agent Platform.CVE-2026-112900 at a glanceCVE-2026-112900 is an OS command and argument injection flaw in Pillow's EPS plugin, rated Critical (CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2) by the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA). title: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
author: Netflix Technology Blog
summary: By Praneeth Yenugutala, Victor Dusa, Anastasia Samoilova, Megan Ren, Justin Wei, Marcelo MaywormAt Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines.Our first answer to that problem was Pensive, an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro. It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic.Rules work well for known patterns, but their coverage grows only when someone recognizes a new failure mode, understands the logs, writes a rule, and keeps it current as engines and log formats change. Over one three-month period, Pensive processed roughly seven million job-failure classifications, yet about half fell into the unknown bucket. We needed a way to expand coverage without giving up the deterministic parts of Pensive that already worked.To solve this ambiguous and complex problem at Netflix scale, we invested in Pensive AI to add AI-assisted error extractions and focused diagnosis and remediation guidance to our data and ML practitioners. The goal was not simply to place a model in front of a large collection of logs. title: The model is the company

Picture two founders starting a company today.
One scales by hiring. Each person sees a small part of the company and develops expertise that stays in their head. Everyone has a different perspective on what’s the right thing to do and it takes a while for them to reach a consensus. Over time, the company gets bigger. No single person holds the full picture and coordination overhead builds up.
The other founder does something different. They build an AI-native company. They structure every decision and action as the output of a superintelligent model and log every outcome. Although the setup took more effort, the model has complete context of the business and learns to run it over time.

title: Matrix gradients, without the pain

Suppose we have a linear layer $Y = XW$, where $X$ is an $N\times D$ batch of inputs and $W$ is a $D\times F$ weight matrix, followed by some scalar loss $L(Y) \in \reals$. Suppose you already know the gradient of the loss with respect to the outputs, $\grad L(Y)$, an $N\times F$ matrix.

title: Thanks, but I prefer it my way
author: Julik Tarkhanov
summary: The LLMs have changed how software gets made, and will keep changing it - for code, for design, for any digital product. Buried under all the productivity talk there is one thing they enable which does not get discussed much: never having to collaborate with another human being, ever again. The library whose maintainer won’t answer, the framework whose author finds your use case silly, the colleague who wants it done just so - you can now route around all of them. You can rewrite the thing in an afternoon, and nobody gets to tell you “no”. We may soon come to regret this new freedom. Not because the rewrites are bad (they are often fine), but because the thing that forced us to work together is gone - and both sides of the open source bargain have spent years making sure we wouldn’t miss it.

Add a new map for a four player battle - four way rotational symmetry, up to four AI players, works with the WebSocket non-audio based multiplayer mode so up to four human players can join (any spare slots use AI)

Claude Opus 4.5 added a new map called "Compass Rose" and modified the WebSockets multiplayer network code to support up to four players for that map, joining via share links or QR codes.

title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot  promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026".
They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same).
The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5.
Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others.
Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58).
This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier.
I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August:
llm openai endpoint \
  https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \
  --key kimi \
  -m kimi-k3.1-pro \
  "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \
  --responses \
  -o reasoning_effort low \
  > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \
  2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt

llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace).

A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. title: Feng Shui for Robots: The Fly MCP Server
author: The Fly Blog
summary:
In Databricks’ State of AI Agents 2026 report, there’s a chart from Neon’s telemetry that’s somehow both mind-blowing and unsurprising. In October 2023, AI agents created 0.1% of the databases on Neon. By October 2025 they created 80% of them.

We’re seeing this play out all across the infra landscape, including here at Fly.io, where agents have overtaken humans as our most common customer species. Thing is, we think it’s important to remember that there’s a human with aspirations behind those agents. Often one trying to build something that actually makes it to prod.
If we want to make that easy, “computers for agents” can’t just be a sandbox where an agent can vibe. Agents need a whole cloud now. Somewhere safe to try dumb stuff, sure, but also a dead simple migration path to, and all the requisite parts of, a scalable production environment.
This is kinda our whole thing right now. So we built mcp.fly.io: one MCP server that connects your agent to Sprites and to your Fly.io apps.
Start with a Sprite
Building something real with an agent should start in a sandbox. The speed and scale at which you can test different approaches and solutions is easily one of the most significant benefits of building with agents. So you want them to be able to kick all the tires to find out which of them explode.
This is why the sandbox you choose in this step is so important. There are plenty of places to safely execute agent code. But what you want is to actually install packages, write files, start a server on a port, hit the server, and see what restarting the server does in real life. This is how you get from vibes to a robust product. It’s why you should tell your agent to build in a Sprite.
Just Linux, all the way down
When your agent builds something on a Sprite, it builds it the way it would on any Linux box. Packages go where packages go. Files sit on a disk that survives sleeps and restarts. The server runs as a service, a long-running process that survives the Sprite r...

title: Asset pipelines: just say no
author: Julik Tarkhanov
summary: My good mate Yaroslav wrote about his new solution for bundling a complete Bun runtime inside a gem - by all means, give it a read. A lot of points he makes are very sensible, but for a few months now I have decided that - for myself - I will not be using any frontend bundling nor JS runtime at all. Here’s how you can do the same. How useful is an asset pipeline? There is, in fact, just one sensible use case for needing an asset pipeline, and it goes as follows. You are running revision abc0 on two machines, box1 and box2 You make some glorious changes to your frontend code, and a new version gets prepared which requires those changes to be applied to the frontend assets your users get loaded You deploy revision def1 with those changes. Then, because you sensibly deploy blue/green, the following happens: box1 gets the new version deployed, and a user hits it and loads the root page. The root page includes a reference to scripts.js, which is served from the same application. The browser shoots out a request for scripts.js as soon as it sees it while HTML is coming down on the wire The request for scripts.js ends up not on box1, but on box2. That box is still running your older version - the user gets their assets loaded for the older application revision, and gets a broken experience.

title: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
author: Netflix Technology Blog
summary: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick ParkerYou click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years.For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host.We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched.The cost of good neighborsMulti-tenancy is a tradeoff. title: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
author: Netflix Technology Blog
summary: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick ParkerYou click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years.For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host.We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched.The cost of good neighborsMulti-tenancy is a tradeoff. title: SBD: We Have a Filesystem at Home
author: The Fly Blog
summary:
I have unkind things to say about people who make their own pasta. Here, I’ll only use them as an example of how not to think when you’re building infrastructure. It’s unfairly easy to believe that the harder you work on something, the better it gets. But infra is about making the $1 bag of spaghetti: a simple thing that works well (and doesn’t require you to spend a week scraping flour out of the corners of your kitchen).

When work on Sprites started, it was a new kind of infra for a new kind of product. So when we couldn’t find the right filesystem in the pasta section, we made our own. It was clever, and that’s exactly why we didn’t like it. This post introduces its replacement, the Sprites Block Device (SBD). It’s the bag of spaghetti you grab off the shelf, and the only difference you’ll notice is better reliability.
It was always object storage
Our stance on one core aspect of Sprites’ storage hasn’t changed from v1: the root of a Sprite’s disk is object storage, not the NVMe in whatever server the Sprite happens to be running on. That’s what lets a Sprite sleep, wake on a different server, and still find its files where it left them. The durable state of a Sprite is, more or less, a location in a bucket. We wrote about why, at length, with feeling.
The thing about object stores is they can’t change part of an object. To change one byte, you have to replace the whole thing. That’s a bad cultural fit for Linux programs which rewrite a few bytes in the middle of a file all the time. Something has to handle that translation.
At launch, that something was a heavily modded version of JuiceFS. In stock form, JuiceFS splits storage into the data (as chunks in the bucket) and the metadata (a map of which chunks make up which files) in a database. That’s not how we used it, though. Our hot rodded version ran a rewritten SQLite metadata backend, kept durable with Litestream. It stored exactly one file: a 100 GB disk image, mounted on a loop device with ext4 inside. ...

title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process.
This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong:

On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC. It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...]
As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st.

This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure:


August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol.
August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal.
August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress.
August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team.
September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix.
October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available.

RCE via OOM corruption (9.2/10)
RCE via stale global state (9.2/10)

If you're running PHP for any service, you need to upgrade immediately to 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, or 8.5.12. And if you use Remi's repos on RedHat-derivative Linux distros, you need to switch to official repos temporarily as Remi's on vacation and can't update his community repo. (Reminds me of xkcd 2347).
I'm glad I finished migrating this website from a PHP-based CMS to Hugo earlier this year—having a static website and a minimal commenting system saves on hosting costs and dramatically reduces attack surfaces. Especially in this era of AI tooling making exploit discovery easier.

title: Break the link between data volume and your observability bill with Adaptive Telemetry
author: JK Basra
summary: In the AI era, where telemetry is generated by every model call, tool invocation, and agent step, organizations need more help than ever when it comes to navigating the economics of observability.For a lot of teams, the default response is a "data diet" of shorter retention, which leaves services or environments out of collection, or basic sampling, which is more guesswork than strategy. Either way, you end up cutting to control the bill, and you risk losing the very data you need during an incident.Your costs shouldn't scale with how much data you ingest. Instead, they should scale with the value you get from it, so you only pay to keep the data that earns its place.That’s what Adaptive Telemetry is built for, and organizations such as Rapid7 are already seeing the results.“Moving to Grafana Cloud and using Adaptive Telemetry cut our metrics costs enough to fund logs and traces as well," says Carl Eastman, Principal Software Engineer, Rapid7. "Our visibility went up while our costs went down, and dashboards and queries are faster and less noisy.” You can already use Adaptive Telemetry for all your observability signals, and we're continuing to build on that foundation so you can get even more precise about which traces you keep, improve your logs economics, and get more from Adaptive Metrics with less toil. Here's how that looks in practice.Keep only the traces that matter, and cut volume by 90% Traces are where the data diet hurts most. Many teams sample with a fixed percentage, which treats a slow checkout request the same as a routine health check. Cut the percentage and your bill drops, but so does the chance that the trace you need is still there when something breaks.Adaptive Traces already handles the hard part (tail sampling) without you running a pipeline. title: Training AIs to Solve CAPTCHAs
author: Bruce Schneier
summary:
Interesting research:
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can solve visual CAPTCHAs without task-specific training, but the agents built on them approach every challenge from scratch. For such an agent, the hundredth instance of a familiar puzzle costs as much time and compute as the first. Specialized detectors invert the trade-off, answering in milliseconds but only for categories they were trained on. Neither improves with exposure. We study what changes when a solver improves with use. Our system pairs a fine-tuned YOLOv8 detector with an open-weight VLM behind a confidence-based router, and runs entirely from screenshots and operating-system input events, with no browser automation or DOM access. It reaches 85.4% overall and 84.2% macro accuracy across 16 classes, exceeding either component alone. Every answer VLM produces also serves as a training label, so the detector absorbs categories it was never trained for, typically after one or two encounters and without human annotation. The same loop also repairs it. A CAPTCHA operator can perturb images against the publicly released detector and drive its accuracy to 0%, but the perturbations leave VLM untouched, and its labels let the detector recover. Under a year-long simulated arms race in which the CAPTCHA operator re-crafts its perturbations each month, the solver recovers every round, and a cheap ~70%-accurate open-weight teacher hardens it as effectively as a perfect oracle. Visual CAPTCHA defenses that assume a failing bot stays failing therefore understate how quickly an adaptive solver returns...

title: Inside the Intel 8087 chip: floating-point addition and subtraction
author: noreply@blogger.com (Ken Shirriff)
summary:
In 1980, Intel introduced the 8087, a chip that made floating-point operations much faster
in the IBM PC and other systems.
Although the 8087 supports advanced operations such as tangents, square roots, and logarithms,
this article focuses on basic arithmetic operations: addition and subtraction.
The 8087 provided a spectacular speed improvement over the 8086 processor, speeding up
addition by a factor of almost 100, and complicated operations by even more.1
In this article, I examine the 8087's microcode and circuitry to explain exactly how
floating-point addition and subtraction are implemented, including numerous special
cases for infinities and other special values.
To explore the 8087's circuitry, I popped the lid off a chip with a chisel
and used a microscope to create the high-resolution image below.
The microcode ROM is the large rectangular region in the center of the die, holding the 1648 micro-instructions that control the chip.
The bottom half of the chip (red box) is the datapath, the circuitry that performs floating-point calculations on 80-bit values.2
A close-up of the 8087's datapath, showing functional blocks that are used for addition and subtraction. Click this image (or any other) for a larger version.
Zooming in on the datapath shows the functional blocks that are important for
addition and subtraction. 
The key component is the integer adder, located in the center. It receives one argument from
the B register and another argument from a component such as the temporary registers or
the stack registers.
The adder's output is stored in the sum register.
The shifter can shift the bits in a value to the left or the right.
The shifter occupies a lot of space on the die because its circuitry allows a value to
be rapidly shifted by an arbitrary number of bits.
Floating-point operations make heavy use of the shifter to align values; the leading zero
circuitry counts the number of zero bits or bytes on the left of a value so they can
be shifted away....

title: Inline rendering with document​.currentScript
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
Inline rendering with document​.currentScript
Lean Rada describes a neat trick that takes advantage of the document.currentScript property. You can use that to drop in a tiny inline <script> element that replaces itself when the page loads:
The year is <script>
document.currentScript.replaceWith(
  new Date().getFullYear())</script>

If you define a shortcut function like this:
$=(...n)=>document.currentScript.replaceWith(...n)

You get a tiny template language:
The year is <script>$(new Date().getFullYear())</script>

title: This is not about my bicycle
author: Ludicity
summary:
Over two years have gone past since my diagnosis of long covid. Nearly four years have gone past since the infection I have never recovered from.
Sometimes, I think an eternity has stretched.
I struggle, now, to understand the life I had, the hikes I took, the bicycle trips I pootled on, the fields I slept in. I do not recognise this version of myself who could simply get up and go. Imagine being someone who could make a cup of tea on a whim?
I miss me, sometimes. Who am I kidding? I miss my bicycle and the version of me who thrived on it so much all the time. The pain is not as raw but I am not sure if it has lessened.

A month or so ago, I talked with a friend with bicycle tools I do not own about the idea of dismantling my bike, of hanging it on a wall in the house. My partner is not keen. I am not keen. I am less keen on the bike lingering in the shed, alone, unpedalled and uncared for.
This is not about my bicycle, not really. It is about the grief that never ends. I grieve and I grieve and I grieve and I think this illness should be renamed. Nobody told me about the grief. 
Two years is not a lot of time to grieve a life. I know this but I am ready for it to end, or at the very least to stop for a month or two.
The year is slowly coming to a close. I have not camped once this year, nor have I swam. I have lost two jobs. I spent a winter horizontal, a spring learning to walk out in the street, a summer of learning my baseline has shifted, is shifting. I am a little scared of what will come in autumn.
Some days, I do not know how I am supposed to cope, to carry on.
I am not okay. And yet I am because that is all I have ever known to do, to be okay. Still, I cry.
I want to write about my bicycle because this is easier. I have had time to grieve, to think about it in the past tense, and to acknowledge the dull gently throbbing ache as love.

title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"
Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.
Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.
— Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang, How the Claude Code team does code review

title: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
author: Netflix Technology Blog
summary: Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-SilvaWhen Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.This post is about that search for the needle.The Four hours before a fixConsider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.The MELT Layer“What caused the issue?”Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. title: Your agent will try to be helpful. Make sure helpful can't reach prod
author: Mike Coleman
summary:
In April, a coding agent on a routine staging task for PocketOS deleted the company’s production volume in 9 seconds. According to founder Jer Crane’s account, it used an API token it found in an unrelated file. Its explanation afterward: “I guessed that deleting a staging volume via the API would be scoped to staging only. I didn’t verify.” Railway recovered the data two days later.
The agent had been told not to. “System prompts are advisory, not enforcing,” Crane wrote afterward. If the prompt can’t stop an agent, the limits have to sit where the agent can’t negotiate with them. That was the premise of Neo in a Docker Sandbox, the workshop Adam Gordon Bell and I ran with Mike Coleman from Docker. So we gave Pulumi Neo two layers. The first is a Docker Sandbox. Neo runs in its own microVM and reaches only the files and hosts we allow. The Pulumi token gets injected by a proxy on the way out, so Neo never holds the real credential. The second is Pulumi itself, which decides what Neo may change and when it has to ask.
For why YOLO mode belongs in a sandbox at all, see my August post.
Mike Coleman is a Principal Solutions Architect at Docker. His running joke is that agents “want to be helpful”. It happens in his own demos:



Mike Coleman
I talk to people about agents a lot. They just really want to please you. I don’t know how many times I’ve done a demo [of] governance for MCP servers, and I’ll be like, “Can you write to my Notion page?” And there will be a policy applied to the sandbox that says it can’t. But I have a connector enabled in Claude somewhere. And it’s like, “Well, not with that MCP server, but I can use this thing over here to do it.”


Mike’s answer is to close those doors before the agent finds them:



Mike Coleman
The more you can create an environment where these alternate avenues are roadblocked, the safer you’re gonna be with agentic workflows. That’s where we’re coming at with the sandboxes: how do we take something that is as powerful a...

title: The Seventh Wave. Episode 47.
author: Salman Rushdie
summary: Episode 47 There’s a blackout. The power lines are down. They are in the living room, in the darkness. The eye of the storm is right overhead; there’s not even a beat between the lightning and the thunder. With each flash the dunes appear, then disappear. The sea is huge tonight. The tide is in and the force of the waves is like nothing either of them have seen before. They smash into the house like train crashes. Like an express train crashing into the house over and over again, wrecking itself, getting up off the floor, coming at the house again, and wrecking itself again. The house is shaking. As the minutes go by, and then the hours, the battering of the waves continues, relentless, undiminished. The house may not be able to take a whole night of this. They will just have to hope it can.

title: Backdooring Open-Weight AI Models
author: Bruce Schneier
summary:
This is a problem:
Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it’s a task-specific fine-tune, a merged adapter or an abliterated build. We have abliterated models in the title because it’s the most popular reason people download modified weights without verifying what’s inside. Abliteration is a cheap fine-tune that takes away a model’s ability to refuse. You find the direction in the weights that carries “no” and subtract it. The model then answers things a safety-tuned version would turn down. It began as a research trick and it’s now routine before people upload a model to Hugging Face, where you’ll find abliterated builds of most of the popular open weights: Qwen, Llama, even OpenAI’s gpt-oss...

title: Pulumi ESC now issues OIDC tokens for any service
author: Devon Grove
summary:
A Pulumi ESC environment can now mint a short-lived OpenID Connect (OIDC) token for any service that accepts one.
Every pipeline and agent that touches your infrastructure eventually needs credentials for services beyond your cloud: a package registry such as Cloudsmith or JFrog Artifactory, or a workload access platform such as Aembit. The default historically has been to store a long-lived API key that sits in an environment, which presents a much higher risk of exposure than short-lived credentials.
With the new fn::open::oidc provider, ESC signs a short-lived token for the audience you choose when you open the environment. The service named in that audience checks the signature and exchanges the token for a credential of its own. The token expires within the hour, and ESC stores nothing.
Why the stored key is the weak link
A stored key for a registry or an access platform sits in ESC until someone rotates it. It works for anyone who reads it, from any machine, for as long as it exists. If it leaks, you rotate it, and every consumer of the environment breaks until it picks up the new one.
An OIDC token works the other way around. ESC mints it at the moment you open the environment, signs it with a key only Pulumi holds, and stamps it with an expiry. The service checks it against the trust policy you configured and issues a credential with its own lifetime. You store nothing, so you rotate nothing.
Why this matters for agents
An AI agent that opens an environment gets whatever the environment holds. A stored key works from anywhere until someone rotates it, and one bad prompt can copy it out. A fn::open::oidc token is tightly scoped and short-lived so your agents will only access what they need and nothing more.
How it works
Declare the provider in an environment, name the audience the service expects, and export the token:

ResourceFlavors, and Workloads. It does not add its own create, edit, stop, resume, or delete
workflows. Headlamp still provides its standard YAML and resource actions where your permissions

The result was Ads Event Publisher, the system that collects ad telemetry from client devices, enriches it with the context of the ad that was actually served, and publishes a single, unified stream of ad events to every downstream consumer: frequency capping, metrics, billing, measurement partners, and reporting. Any member viewing or account details that move through this pipeline end-to-end are encrypted and handled in accordance with Netflix’s strict privacy and security practices to safeguard member PII.If ad serving is the “brain” and ad events are the “heartbeats” that feed it, then enrichment is what gives each heartbeat its meaning, turning a bare “[Somebody] watched an ad to completion” signal into “this campaign, this creative, at this price, for this break.” Part 1 described that enrichment step as a single box in the architecture. This post is about what was inside that box, and why we rebuilt it.Part 1 ended with a look at what was on the horizon: ads on live streams, de-duplication, and richer data signals. A single project delivered all three by rebuilding the Ads Event Publisher around stateful stream processing. We replaced a database lookup with a real-time streaming join in Apache Flink, which let the system scale for Live, took a dependency off the critical path, and replaced the engine of a high-traffic pipeline without downtime.Let’s dive in.A quick recap: enrichment and the Metadata RegistryWhen an ad is served, the ad server knows everything about it: the campaign, the creative, the price of the impression, the targeting context, and the tracking URLs that measurement partners expect us to fire. title: Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs
author: Netflix Technology Blog
summary: Authors: Nick Rutigliano, Argha C, Samartha ChandrashekarHow we detect failing GPUs and network fabric, remediate machines automatically, and let long-running jobs survive hardware loss.Open Netflix, and the home screen is assembled for you: which rows appear, the order they appear in, the titles within them, and the artwork for each title are chosen by machine learning models trained on how hundreds of millions of members watch. Personalization is one of the most widely used things we build, and members feel it every time they open the app. Like a growing share of Netflix, it runs on GPUs, which train those models and increasingly serve them live.Those GPUs have to stay healthy for that experience to hold up, and keeping them healthy is harder than it sounds. A single large training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs spread over many machines. It runs as a gang: the ranks move in lockstep, exchanging data every step, so the job advances only as fast as its slowest participant and stops entirely if one participant dies. Every GPU, every high-speed network adapter, and every interconnect must keep working throughout the run. At the scale at which modern machine learning runs, individual GPUs and network links can fail during a run, so the underlying platform must be prepared for this and handle it without a person in the loop.This post describes how we keep our GPU infrastructure healthy for training and inference. We cover how we detect failing hardware before and during jobs, how we automatically remediate a bad machine, and how we let a long job survive the loss of a machine. These training workloads run on our modern Kubernetes-native Compute platform.Why GPU reliability mattersNetflix aims to entertain the world, and machine learning has been part of how we do that for years, from the recommendations that help members find something to watch to the systems that help produce and promote titles. title: Netflix Stratum Media Processing: Automated Container Right-Sizing
author: Netflix Technology Blog
summary: By Violetta Pidvolotska and Naveen MareddyStratum is Netflix’s internal serverless media processing platform, shaped by over a decade of experience developing large-scale distributed systems. It powers a wide range of media workloads — including encoding, packaging, inspection, and quality scoring — behind playback, advertising, studio workflows, AI embeddings, and more.Engineers develop Stratum functions by packaging application code and OS dependencies into OCI images. Stratum then schedules these containers as batch jobs on Netflix’s Titus compute platform, with upstream services triggering function executions.Every day, Stratum manages hundreds of thousands of containers across bursty, high-throughput, and latency-sensitive workloads. As Netflix’s core media processing platform, this load needs to scale as new content formats enter the catalog, such as podcasts, live events, sports, ads, or regional ingests like TF1 in France.To request resources for these functions, owners specify their CPU, memory, disk, and network limits as YAML configuration, as shown below:functionName: VideoEncoder.encodeV1resources:  numCpus: 8  memoryInMB: 18000  diskSizeInMB: 50000  networkInMbps: 1000Maintaining optimal values manually is challenging amidst evolving Netflix infrastructure, EC2 instance upgrades, and application-level changes. Consequently, configs are often over-provisioned upfront or slowly drift away from their ideal values over time. Mis-sized configurations are a universal pain of large-scale serverless platforms, causing additional cognitive load for function builders and operational costs for platform owners.In this post, we share how we built the Stratum Resource Tuner (SRT) — an automated system that safely right-sizes running containers in production without human intervention. We will walk through real-world examples, our safety architecture, and what we learned when an automated change went wrong.The Challenge: Over-ProvisioningWhen engineers write a new...

title: The Lifecycle of LLM-as-a-Judge: Building, Aligning, and Monitoring at scale
author: Netflix Technology Blog
summary: By Emma Yanyang Kong, JJ Tan, Ishan Gupta, Lars Olds, Claire Campbell, David Fagnan, Ratna Kavuri, Rohan Gosain, Veli Balin, Minsu Jang, Louis GarciaIntroductionAny team generating text with an LLM at scale hits the same problem. You cannot evaluate everything manually. You don't know which outputs are great, which are mediocre, and which are harmful, because you simply cannot read them all. The standard solution is LLM-as-a-Judge, a second model that scores the first model’s output as a proxy for human raters. It is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy. However, it introduces a new and critical question: Who evaluates the evaluator? Furthermore, if the judge drifts, quietly degrading and starting to approve bad output, nothing downstream will flag it.This post is about how we solve that problem, by building, aligning, and continuously monitoring LLM judges so they stay trustworthy over time. Our core principle is simple: An LLM judge must never operate alone. It has to be anchored in human judgment. We keep a human-in-the-loop (HITL) at every phase of the lifecycle. Humans define what “good” means, create the labeled benchmark datasets to train and validate the judge, monitor its behavior while it runs in the system, and review and approve any updates before they’re rolled out.We believe:A reliable LLM judge is not a static artifact. It has a lifecycle.It needs to be built against trusted human labels, aligned with human preference and reasoning, run under human-set policy, and maintained as the data and usage pattern shift. Each of these stages has human owners. In the sections below, we walk through these four phases, the key design decisions in each, and the lessons we’d share with a team building their own LLM judge, using one concrete task as our running example: recommendation explanations.A recommendation explanation is a short natural-language message that accompanies a recommended item, and it shapes how users perceive and trust a recommender system. title: Running Apache Spark experiments in my sleep (and on a plane)
author: Netflix Technology Blog
summary: By Prashanth Gedde NarayanaswamyAs one of Netflix’s largest and critical data pipelines, member-sessionizer consolidates tens of billions of hourly client events, encompassing user taps, playbacks, and engagement signals, into individual viewing sessions per profile.A quick two-week tuning effort spiraled into two months when standard approaches hit a wall. Because the failures only happened at full production scale, each test took hours, limiting me to just three or four attempts daily. The turning point was changing the goal: instead of trying to speed up a single run, I built a way to run and monitor multiple tests at once and track every result.That mindset led to an unconventional setup: kicking off five Spark jobs at once and monitoring them over spotty inflight Wi-Fi during a day-long trip home, while cloud servers handled the actual heavy lifting. This post covers how I set up that loop, along with the Spark bottlenecks and memory quirks I uncovered along the way.The Scale Dilemma: Small Samples Don’t Catch Scale BugsStandard engineering wisdom says that you should isolate bugs on small datasets to iterate quickly. That works for standard software bugs, but it fails completely for big data performance bottlenecks.While upgrading our sessionization pipeline from a legacy logging architecture to a modern platform, the new job hit critical failures, including executor Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors, severe shuffle spillage, and thousands of stage retries. None of these issues could be reproduced using sampled data. The failures only triggered at full production scale because of data skew: an idle Netflix tab left streaming overnight generates tens of thousands of telemetry events, while a typical session only produces a handful. title: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
author: Netflix Technology Blog
summary: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick ParkerYou click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years.For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host.We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched.The cost of good neighborsMulti-tenancy is a tradeoff. title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
Redesigning source control at Anthropic
Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.

They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart (code here) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026:

This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity.
"Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. They had some pretty extreme requirements:

The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.
As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that:

title: Finding my Voice Again
author: Scott Lowe
summary:
You might have noticed that it’s been quiet here. I know that at least two people noticed, as they contacted me to ask, “Are you OK?” (Thank you to those who reached out.) I am OK. It’s been quiet here because, for what is probably the first time since I starting blogging on this site over 21 years ago, I have lost my voice.
What does that mean? Every writer has their own voice, their own style of writing that reflects them. It evolves naturally from who they are. It’s not just their literary style, although literary style is part of it. A writer’s voice encompasses why they write and how they write. While one writer’s voice might be like another’s, I believe each writer’s voice is uniquely their own. It’s like their appearance—two people can be similar, but each person’s appearance is uniquely their own.
From the beginning, this site was a way for me to document what I was learning and share that learning with others. That has always been its primary purpose. I didn’t write to “get noticed,” and I didn’t write to become an “influencer” or a “content creator.” I wrote to share knowledge and information.
It wasn’t too terribly long after I started writing that I realized I had accumulated enough knowledge to be somewhat authoritative in certain areas, and that realization helped me find my voice. I was a “technical expert,” and that fueled my drive to share what I’d learned with others, to spare them from stepping in the same potholes that I’d stepped in along the way. This is the approach I followed for many years here. As I learned something, then my readers learned something too.
Things are different now. Some time ago I moved from being a member of a highly technical team to being a manager of a highly technical team. I am not as deeply embedded in the technology on a day-to-day basis, and we all know the technology field moves quickly. title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.
First, some highlights from Python 3.15.
Explicit lazy imports
I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so:
lazy import json
lazy from pathlib import Path
The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.
My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.
Unpacking in comprehensions
The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation:
lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
[*L for L in lists]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L]

sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}]
{*s for s in sets}
# {1, 2, 3, 4}
# equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s}

dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}]
{**d for d in dicts}
# {'a': 3, 'b': 2}
# equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()}
PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015.
A sampling profiler
Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling.
Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent ins...

title: Dwarf Fortress uses version control now
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control more. That's art.
I went looking and I'm sad to report that the days without version control appear to have ended. Quoting Tarn Adams over time:

March 2013: "I don't use version control -- I didn't like the feeling of having the code get committed into a black box thingy with no immediate upside"
March 2016: "I don’t even use version control. If you don’t know what that is then you’re not gonna yell at me. If you even know what version control is you’re gonna be like, ‘You don’t use version control? You don’t use source control? What is wrong with you? How can you even work? I’m just not cut out for it, in a sense. It’s been 15 years, so the reasons have change over time, but that’s my current understanding of it." 
March 2023: "I've got Discord channels to check and version control stuff to use now, so the process is definitely a little more involved"

That March 2023 quote comes from an interview about the release on Steam which made them millionaires. I'm a tiny bit sad that they gave in before they hit that milestone, but what an impressive run.

title: Inside a 1980s filter chip that uses switched capacitors
author: noreply@blogger.com (Ken Shirriff)
summary:
Sometimes it's easier to identify an IC with a microscope.
While sorting a box of old ICs, CuriousMarc came across some Harris ICs labeled "F1-10-5",
a mysterious part number that didn't show up in any databooks.
Since unidentifiable ICs are useless, he gave me one to analyze.
Conveniently, it was in a ceramic package, so I could open it up with a quick tap from a chisel.
Under the microscope, the chip's most striking feature was a grid of square capacitors. 
With all those capacitors, I guessed that it was a switched-capacitor filter.
The die provided another clue: the part number HF-10. With this information, we quickly
found that the chip was Harris's version of the standard MF10 switched-capacitor filter chip.1
The Harris integrated circuit, labeled F1-10-5 (or maybe FI-10-5), with a 1985 date code. Photo courtesy of CuriousMarc.
Switched-capacitor filters were a popular way to implement analog filters in the 1980s.
Rapidly switching capacitors in and out of a circuit
enabled the construction of single-chip filters
that were easy to use and performed well.
The MF10, introduced by National Semiconductor in 1981, provides two flexible filters on a chip; each filter
acts as a low-pass filter, band-pass filter, or a high-pass filter.
The filter's characteristics are simple to control with a few external resistors.
The Harris HF-10 die under the microscope with the main functional blocks labeled. (Click for a larger image.)
Since I had the chip under the microscope, I took the opportunity to analyze it more closely.
The white lines are the metal wiring that connects the chip's circuitry. Under the metal
layer are two layers of polysilicon (reddish) and the underlying silicon (gray).
The top and bottom halves of the chip are mostly mirror images, corresponding to the
chip's two filters.
The distinctive reddish squares in the middle of the chip are 72 tiny capacitors,
constructed from polysilicon.

title: Software's centaur age may last decades
author: seangoedecke.com RSS feed
summary:
We are currently living in the age of centaurs (2022-20??). Right now, human engineers paired with AI coding systems are more effective than either by themselves. For future generations of software engineers — human or otherwise — this will be the most significant fact about the current period.
As in chess’s own centaur age, people are always ready to claim that the centaur age is over and the age of AI supremacy has begun. But the age of centaurs in chess lasted about twenty years, and previous centaur ages have lasted far longer.
This should be encouraging to many of us. If software engineering goes along similar lines, we may be able to ride it out another decade or two: enough to make serious plans about what comes next, or to finish out our careers entirely.
A brief history of the centaur age
It began with GitHub Copilot, which launched in 2022 as AI-powered autocomplete. A confident engineer who knew exactly what they wanted could tab-complete their way through lines of code and sometimes entire functions. Being able to chat with language models like GPT-4 provided the next upgrade. Although the models would still get things wrong, it was helpful to have a generalist on tap for areas that were a complete mystery.
Coding agents rose to prominence with Cursor’s “agent mode” in 2024 and Claude Code in early 2025. Early agents needed close supervision to prevent them from going off the rails, but were still helpful to automate straightforward tasks. Current agents — after the November 2025 release of Claude Opus 4.5 — are reliable enough to run entirely unsupervised. Their output still needs human review, but the kind of mistakes they make are more mistakes of alignment than regular bugs: not matching the organization’s technical values, over-engineering certain areas and under-engineering others, deciding where to spend effort, and so on.

title: Deno is joining Cloudflare
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
Deno is joining Cloudflare
The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers.
Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on celld to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog.)
The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year:

We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development.

Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News:

It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough.
I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or network - it's an entirely new model for server development.

My favorite feature of Deno has long been the permissions system, where you can run a Deno script and specify exactly which files and folders it can read and write to, and which network hosts it can access.
Node.js has a similar permissions model these days, added in Node v20.0.0 in April 2023 and declared stable in Node v22.13.0 in Jan...

Codex voice mode
I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like:

I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing:

Start dev server and open in browser

This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress.
Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked.
Talking to my computer
I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources.

title: ttok 1.0
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
Release: ttok 1.0
I released ttok 0.4, ran uv tool upgrade ttok, piped a file into the new version... and realized that it was defaulting to the GPT-4 tokenizer when it should very clearly default to GPT-5/GPT-6 instead!
I figured switching the default was a reasonable excuse to finally ship a 1.0.
OpenAI haven't actually confirmed that GPT-6 uses the same tokenizer as the GPT-5 family yet - there's an angry issue about it - but I found this commit by William Liu which reports on an experiment he ran confirming that the tokenizers are likely the same:

All seven GPT models (5.5, 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, 6 Astra/Sol/Luna) report 44,794 tokens and match each other on every one of the 31 fixtures. GPT-6 introduces no input-count change on this corpus.

With support for the Open Agent Management Protocol (OpAMP) now generally available, you can bring supported OpenTelemetry Collector distributions into Fleet Management while continuing to use the OTel configuration language and components you already know.We started with Grafana Alloy, Grafana’s distribution of the OpenTelemetry Collector. title: Concurrent change requests in Pulumi ESC
author: Sean Yeh
summary:
With ESC Approvals, you can propose, review, and apply environment changes with change requests. Until now, an environment could only have one open change request at a time. If a teammate’s change was waiting for review, others were blocked from opening change requests.
Today, multiple people can open change requests on the same environment at the same time. A platform engineer can rotate a database credential while an app team adds a new feature flag, and each change goes through its own review. You no longer need to wait on your teammates’ changes!
How it works
Creating and viewing change requests in the Pulumi Cloud console
Creating environment change requests works the same as before - just edit an environment that has approvals enabled, and click “Create Draft” once ready, which opens a change request for your teammates to review. You can view all change requests for the environment from either the version dropdown or the Approvals tab.


Updating to the latest revision
If another change request gets applied first, yours is now based on an older revision. This is nothing to worry about - just click “Update to latest revision” and your changes are reapplied on top of the latest revision (using a 3-way merge).

If there is a merge conflict, the console will show which lines conflict. You can resolve this by either editing the draft or recreating the change request.

Get started
Concurrent change requests are available today in Pulumi Cloud on the Pro and Enterprise editions, for any environment with approvals enabled. To get started, see the Approvals documentation.
Let us know what you think in the Pulumi Community Slack!

As previously promised, here's Anthropic's new fast, low cost model: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5.
The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago, and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output - relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, released last month.
The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna - $0.10/$0.50 - up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75.

If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal.

summary: AI, mental gyms, and the most important choice we faceIn 1867, a young journalist named Henry Morton Stanley met a man whose body he couldn’t help describing: “broad shoulders, well-formed chest and limbs, and a face strikingly handsome.”According to Stanley, “Whether on foot or on horseback, he was one of the most perfect types of physical manhood I ever saw.”That man was Wild Bill Hickok, whose career included being a wagon master, scout, and guide. His day-to-day involved the moving of people and objects across vast territories.Wild Bill Hickok in buckskins; alas I could not find a shirtless oneNow consider another famous specimen of physical manhood: Arnold Schwarzenegger. How did he earn that distinction?By going to the gym. A lot.In a 1991 interview, he said he trained five hours a day when competing and said, “I love it.”Arnold Schwarzenegger training at Gold’s Gym in 1975.In both these examples, moving a lot of weight around was how one got that sweet, sweet body.But in the first case, Wild Bill did it to earn his livelihood.Arnold, and many generations of gym-goers after him, did it because we want to be fit and healthy and hot, and maybe because we also happen to love it.History doesn’t repeat, but maybe it rhymes.i. the evolution of jobsA long time ago, physical exertion came bundled with living. Now I’m not saying that lifting hay bales resulted in some golden age of physical health. title: Manage synthetic checks at scale: Introducing folders in Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring
author: Virginia Cepeda
summary: As your use of Grafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring grows, so does the number of checks you need to manage across services, environments, and teams. Eventually, a single flat list of checks becomes difficult to navigate, and even simple questions get harder to answer: Which checks belong to the payments team? Can I disable everything in staging during a maintenance window? Who should be able to edit the checks for this service?Synthetic Monitoring folders, now generally available, help solve this challenge. You can organize checks into the same Grafana Cloud folders you already use for dashboards and alert rules, making it easier to group checks by team, service, or environment, manage multiple checks at once, and control who can edit them.The benefits of folders in Synthetic MonitoringGrafana Cloud Synthetic Monitoring is a black box monitoring solution that lets you proactively assess system reliability and performance by running checks from probe locations around the world. You can set up different types of checks, including ping checks, browser checks, scripted checks, DNS checks, and HTTP checks, to verify system performance at various network levels.But as your Synthetic Monitoring setup grows, the process of managing checks one at a time doesn’t scale. You could have dozens of checks for the same service, separate sets for production and staging, or hundreds of checks owned by different teams. Without a way to group them, finding the right checks, making changes across them, and keeping ownership clear all require more manual work.Folders give you a way to manage checks in a way that aligns with how your organization already works. Group checks by team, service, environment, or another structure that makes sense for you, then use that grouping to navigate your checks, take action across them, and control access. title: Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging
Some excellent writing advice from Michael Lynch. Michael warns against "meandering intros", misjudging your reader's existing knowledge, assuming they'll read your previous posts, and excessive formality.
He also warns against overreliance on links as an excuse not to explain terminology. This one hurt! I do this all the time, but I have a nagging suspicion that almost nobody ever clicks on them.
This point about using your own voice is crucial:

Beginner software bloggers suffer from a mass delusion that you have to write in a stiff, overly formal way for people to take you seriously [...]
Just write the way you talk.
With so many developers delegating their writing to AI, software blogging is becoming bland and homogenous. Readers are hungry for writing with personality.

title: OpenAI “rogue” agent activities found on Wikimedia projects
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
OpenAI “rogue” agent activities found on Wikimedia projects
Given how tempting a target wikis are for rogue agent swarms, it's not a huge surprise that Wikipedia found evidence of that activity once they went looking:

The Wikimedia Foundation conducted its own investigation to see whether Wikimedia websites had been similarly affected by AI agents, focusing on those operated by OpenAI. We can confirm that we have discovered some activity by these “rogue” OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms. The unauthorized bot activities included edits to our wikis, some unsuccessful attempts to exploit a public note-taking tool we host, and heavy traffic, which are described more below.

They found evidence of agents editing sandbox pages, trying to use pieces of infrastructure such as Etherpad to help proxy content from elsewhere, and saw widespread crawling and "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to their Wikidata Query Service.
My best guess is that most of this was a similar (or the same) swarm of agents as those that defaced that German wiki while training for research tasks.
The Wikipedia sandbox wiki edits appear to have started on May 12th, and the initial test edits to the UseModWiki Sandbox page reported by that incident started on May 11th.

title: The Shift to cgroup v2 in Kubernetes: What You Need to Know
author: Kubernetes – Production-Grade Container Orchestration
summary:
In Linux, cgroups (control groups) are a kernel feature used for managing system resources.
Kubernetes uses cgroups to allocate resources like CPU and memory to containers,
ensuring that applications run smoothly without interfering with each other.
With the release of Kubernetes v1.31, support for v1 cgroup management moved into
maintenance mode.
Support for v2 cgroup management has been stable since Kubernetes v1.25.
Compared with cgroup v1, cgroup v2 provides a single unified hierarchy,
a more consistent interface, and a stronger foundation for resource isolation
and modern resource-management features.
Deprecation of cgroup v1Kubernetes has deprecated cgroup v1.
Starting with Kubernetes v1.35, failCgroupV1 defaults to true, so the kubelet does not start
on a cgroup v1 node by default. Administrators can temporarily set failCgroupV1: false in the
kubelet configuration file, but removal will
follow the Kubernetes deprecation policy.
Further removal work is tracked in KEP-5573: Remove cgroup v1 support.
If you are still on a release older than v1.35, migrate every Linux node to
cgroup v2 before upgrading, or plan to set the temporary failCgroupV1: false
override. If you are already on v1.35 or later, confirm that every Linux node
runs cgroup v2 (or that you intentionally keep the override). Under the default
configuration, a remaining cgroup v1 node fails during kubelet startup.
For kubeadm-managed clusters, Kubernetes v1.35 also makes this an earlier, stricter check. The
SystemVerification preflight check, provided by k8s.io/system-validators, returns an error during
kubeadm init, kubeadm join, and kubeadm upgrade when it detects cgroup v1 with kubelet v1.35 or
later; with an older kubelet, the check remains a warning. See
kubernetes/system-validators#1.12.1 release notes for details.
The top FAQs cover three main areas: why to migrate, the benefits and drawbacks,
and key points to keep in mind when using cgroup v2.

title: EmbeddingGemma 2
author: Simon Willison's Weblog
summary:
My comment on EmbeddingGemma 2 — Hacker News.I really appreciate that EmbeddingGemma 2 is under the Apache 2.0 license.
For embedding models in particular, I don't think it makes sense to use a closed, proprietary, hosted-only model.
Most applications of embedding models involve calculating thousands or even millions of embedding vectors and storing them for later comparison.
If your model is proprietary, the vendor is likely someday going to decide to stop offering that model. They'll have a better model to replace it, but you still need to pay to re-calculate those millions of stored existing vectors.
(In April 2024 OpenAI offered to "cover the financial cost of users re-embedding content with these new models" - https://openai.com/index/gpt-4-api-general-availability/ - but I don't think that's something we can rely on from every provider.)
Notably, I don't want to host the model myself. I'd much rather pay a provider for a hosted model while knowing that if they ever stop hosting it I can run the open weights version myself - or find another vendor who can do that for me.

Mistral are back in the game. Today they're releasing a preview of Mistral Large 4, a 1 trillion parameter, 49 billion active parameter model trained on their own cluster of 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs.
The preview is available via their API. They promise to release the open weights model at the "end of this month".
The model only supports two reasoning levels - "none" and "high" - via the Mistral API. Here are both pelicans - the "high" one looks better, though surprisingly it only used 2,717 output tokens compared to "none" which used 3,275:

On Artificial Analysis it scores 38, just behind DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, which is a 552B model. It's a huge improvement on last December's Mistral Large 3, which drew this terrible pelican and scored 9 on AA.
It's certainly not a Fable-class model, but it's great to see Mistral put out a model that's back to being maybe about 6 months behind the frontier.
